article_text:
Archives – November 2, 2022

German photographer Ilse Bing (1899-1998) has secured her place as one of the major photographers of the 20th century. Her pioneering images during the inter-war era reveal a modern vision influenced by the impact of both the Bauhaus and Surrealism. Alongside her personal work she produced images in the fields of photojournalism, architectural photography, advertising and fashion, and her work was published in the major magazines of the period and exhibited in France and Germany. She moved from Frankfurt to Paris in 1931 but when the city was taken by the Germans during World War II she and her husband, who were both Jews, were expelled and interned in the South of France. They emigrated to New York in 1941 and she lived there until her death in 1998.

Since the 1970s when she first exhibited at MOMA, New York, there has been a burgeoning interest in her work and, more generally, in European photography of the 1920s and 1930s. As one of the key creative forces of the period Bing became a frequent speaker on the photography of that time and on the development of modern art.

This book, published in association with Fundacion MAPFRE, coincides with a comprehensive retrospective of her work being shown in Madrid by MAPFRE from September 2022 to January 2023. The book offers a chronological and thematic survey of her intense creative career and includes over 160 photographs as well as texts by leading experts Juan Vicente Aliaga, Benjamin Buchloh and Donna West Brett.

Ilse Bing with texts by Juan Vicente Aliaga Benjamin Buchloh And Donna West Brett

I was fortunate to have a photography teacher, Susan Maguire, who encouraged me to take that desire seriously. That encouragement stayed with me throughout my life. My journey wasn’t a straight line. I studied photography at Miami Dade Community College and Florida International University before earning my MFA at Columbia University. Along the way, I developed a strong technical foundation, eventually working as a biomedical photographer and establishing the Medical Photography Department at Baptist Health Systems in 1989. That experience taught me to look closely, to be patient, and to understand the power of a photograph to reveal something we might otherwise overlook. But my deepest interest has always been in using photography to explore the human condition—our vulnerability, mortality, identity, and the things we carry with us through life. For more than four decades, I’ve photographed people, places, and traditions that speak to these concerns. Much of my work comes from my own experiences, my family history, and my ongoing search to understand where I come from and how memory shapes who we are. Teaching photography at Miami Dade College has also become an important part of my photographic journey. My students continually challenge me to look at photography differently and remind me why I fell in love with it in the first place. Receiving the Callanan Excellence in Teaching Award in 2019, which honors photography educators nominated by students or colleagues, affirms the work I continue doing in the classroom. Yet, at its core, what motivates me as both a teacher and an artist remains the same thing that drew me to photography as a young man: the desire to look more closely, to ask questions, and to make photographs that help me understand something about myself and the world around me."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ES: Did you have an influential photography mentor or teacher? What was their biggest impact on you as both an artist and a teacher? TC: Without a doubt, one of the most influential people in my life was Susan Maguire, my high school photography teacher. I was a young man who wanted to become an artist but didn’t really know what that meant or whether it was even possible. Susan introduced me to the work of great photographers through books and helped me understand that photography could be much more than making a beautiful picture. It could be a way of thinking, a way of telling stories, and a way of understanding the world. What I remember most, however, was her generosity and the faith she placed in me. When I finally managed to buy an enlarger but couldn’t afford a lens for it, she lent me one of hers every weekend. That might seem like a small gesture, but to me, it meant everything. She was helping me pursue something I could barely afford to dream about. Years later, when I published my first monograph, The Precipice, I dedicated the book to her. I wanted her to know that her encouragement had stayed with me all those years. I think Susan also shaped the kind of teacher I try to be today. I know what it feels like to be a young student with a passion but very little certainty about the future. I try to recognize that in my own students. Sometimes, what a student needs most is not another technical lesson but someone who believes in them and encourages them to keep going. I can teach students how to use a camera, understand light, and make stronger photographs. But I also hope to give them something Susan gave me: the confidence to believe that what they want to do with their lives is possible. I don’t think there is a greater gift a teacher can give a student."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ES: You have exhibited widely, published books and zines and won many prestigious awards in photography, including the Guggenheim Fellowship (congratulations), how do you share your experience and success as an artist with your students? TC: I think one of the most important things I can share with my students is that being an artist is not just about making photographs. It’s about commitment, curiosity, discipline, and being willing to pursue something even when the path isn’t always clear. I try to lead by example. I continue to make work, apply for grants, publish books, exhibit, and put myself in situations where I have to take risks and learn something new. I want my students to understand that you never stop being a student yourself. I also believe it’s important to show them that there are real opportunities to make a living in photography. Although receiving the Guggenheim Fellowship was a pivotal moment in my career, I see that recognition as more than a personal accomplishment. It gives me an opportunity to encourage my students to take their own work seriously, believe in what they are doing, and understand that their voices matter. Ultimately, I want my students to leave my classroom with more than technical skills. I want them to develop the confidence to pursue their own ideas, the discipline to keep working, and the understanding that a meaningful life in photography is possible. If I can help even one student find the courage to follow that path, I feel I’ve done something worthwhile."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ES: What’s next for you as an artist? I’m interested in what happens to our memories and our sense of belonging as the landscape around us changes. The project is personal, but I think it also speaks to something much larger about how we live and what we leave behind. I’m also working on Scarred , a project exploring the visible and invisible scars people carry. I’m photographing individuals and pairing their portraits with handwritten accounts of their experiences. I’m interested in the stories behind those scars, the things we carry with us, and the ways pain shapes who we become. I hope the project creates a space for empathy and reminds us that, despite our differences, we share more than we realize. These are subjects I keep returning to because I don’t think I’ve exhausted what they have to teach me. At this stage in my career, I also want to be more intentional about bringing my work into the world—seeking exhibition opportunities, placing my photographs in collections, continuing to publish (my next photobook will be published by L’Artiere), and connecting with people who might recognize something of their own experiences in my work. TC: I actually don’t give my students traditional photography assignments where I tell them what to photograph. I believe they already have something incredibly valuable to work with: their own lives, their experiences, their families, their neighborhoods, and the things that interest or concern them. My job is to help them recognize the possibilities in what is already around them. I encourage them to be curious, to slow down, to look more carefully, and to ask themselves why something matters to them. Sometimes the most meaningful photographs come from subjects they’ve known their entire lives but have never really learned to see. Of course, I teach them the technical aspects of photography, visual literacy, and how to make decisions about light, composition, time, and perspective. We spend a great deal of time looking at photographs, discussing them, and participating in critiques. I want students to understand not only how to make a photograph, but also why they are making it. I think it’s important that students develop their own voices rather than simply learn to satisfy a teacher’s expectations. When they photograph something personal, something they genuinely care about, the work often becomes more honest and meaningful. They begin to discover things about themselves in the process. For me, teaching is less about giving students answers and more about helping them ask better questions. I want them to leave my classroom understanding that photography isn’t just about pointing a camera at something. It’s about learning to see, finding meaning in the world around them, and discovering what they have to say about it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ES: What is the most meaningful part of your job? I believe my responsibility as a teacher is to give students the tools they need to think for themselves, make their own decisions, and develop their own voices. At some point, the umbilical cord must be cut, and I believe that needs to happen sooner rather than later. My goal isn’t to create students who depend on me for answers. It’s to help them develop the confidence to ask their own questions, take risks, make mistakes, and learn from them. I’m proud of what they’ve accomplished, but what means the most to me is knowing that they have found their own paths. Their success reminds my current students that studying photography can lead to real opportunities, and that there isn’t just one way to build a meaningful career. Teaching has also taught me that I can’t measure my success by how much my students depend on me. I measure it by their ability to move forward without me. When a former student no longer needs my guidance, but still chooses to come back, share their experiences, or help the next generation, that’s incredibly rewarding. Ultimately, I hope my students leave my classroom with more than the ability to make good photographs. I want them to have the curiosity, discipline, and independence to navigate the world on their own terms. He is certainly the most challenging professor I have ever had the pleasure of studying under. His passion is infectious, and always motivated me to do my best, not only in class, but in my personal life. He has an obvious passion for photography, yes, but his devotion to education is what sets him apart. His knowledge is an inspiration and a goal. The goal is not to photograph and think the way he does, the goal is to use the way we think to inspire our images and visual narratives. He adapts his teaching style to match each student’s preferred learning method, molding us to be the photographers we want to be. Although he does not sugarcoat things, his honesty is what has taught me the most about photography. He makes learning fun whilst always maintaining a deep respect for the craft. A master in his field, and still a humble and caring individual. Tony Chirinos is the model of what a true professor should be. I am a better photographer and a better person because I met him, and for that I am forever grateful."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lorena Marrero IG: @lorenalmarrero", "links": [{"text": "@lorenalmarrero", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/lorenalmarrero/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Jaider_Moreno_LENSCRATCH_3.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Jaider Moreno"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Jaider_Moreno_LENSCRATCH_6.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Jaider Moreno"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Jaider_Moreno_LENSCRATCH_7.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Jaider Moreno"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I first met Tony back in Fall of 2022; I didn’t know what to expect. I still remember the first day I met him, he showed me around the darkroom and that was it, I got bit by the photography bug. It was the beginning of many days in that darkroom, a place that I genuinely consider my sanctuary. Being a part of the photographic program at Miami Dade College Kendall has helped me grow not only as a photographer but also as person, and I have no other than Tony Chirinos to thank for that. His passion, respect and work ethic for photography and its practice is something I admire and work hard at to implement in my life. I try to be a sponge and absorb as much of his knowledge of photography and its history as I possibly can. One of the many things I admire about Tony is that he truly and deeply cares about his students and wants us to grow. When I first began taking photo classes with him, I was (and to a certain extent still am) a very shy person, but Tony saw something in me that I had not seen in myself. When he asked me to be President of the Photo Club at MDC Kendall, I was hesitant at first to say yes but seeing that Tony believed in me and saw that I had the potential to lead, it shifted something inside me, something that I’ve carried with me ever since then. That decision changed the trajectory of my life. Tony has not only been my professor and mentor; he’s also been like a father to me. It’s an honor and privilege to know him."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Jadier Moreno IG: @jaider.m", "links": [{"text": "@jaider.m", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/jaider.m/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tony Chirinos is a Venezuelan-born documentary-style artist based in Miami. His career spans over forty years, exploring the theme of mortality and fragility. Chirinos is a recipient of fellowships including the prestigious John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation (2023), The Green Space Miami Grant (2024), Callanan Excellence in Teaching Award (2019), the South Florida Cultural Consortium (2010), and the William Talbott Hillman Foundation grant (2021) to financially assist in the printing production of his first monograph, “The Precipice.” Mr. Chirinos holds a Master of Fine Arts from Columbia University (2003). Trained as a Bio-medical photographer in 1985 at Miami Children’s Hospital, he went on to create the Medical Photography department at Baptist Health Systems in 1989. His work has been exhibited nationally and internationally, including participation in the III Bronx Latin American Art Biennial. article_text:
Photography Educator: Tony Chirinos

©Tony Chirinos, Jaider, from the project Scarred

Photography Educator is a monthly series on Lenscratch that highlights outstanding photography teachers who inspire students of all ages. Each month, the series celebrates an educator’s insights, strategies, and excellence in fostering creativity and resilience.

For the month of November, I am honored to feature artist and educator Tony Chirinos whose work has shaped conversations around the fragility and strength of the human body and spirit. A fellow educator introduced me to Tony’s practice last year, and I had the pleasure of meeting him in person a few weeks ago at CENTER ’s Review Santa Fe. Tony also serves on CENTER’s board.

Deep curiosity and personal experience with death and impermanence guide his photography, resulting in images that are visually compelling and rich in meaning. With poetic grace, his work deepens my understanding of mortality and dying. As professor of photography at Miami Dade College for more than twenty years, Tony brings that same curiosity and commitment to his students, cultivating their creative growth and individual perspectives.

This article features a selection of Tony’s photographs from two projects Scarred and What the Land Remembers , reflections and photographs from some of his students, and an interview exploring his path as an educator and photographer. Together, these offer a window into the lasting impact of his artistic and educational practice.

In Tony’s words: Photography holds the power to convey deep emotion and tell compelling stories. My artistic vision is rooted in personal experience, guiding me to create documentary-style projects that explore ongoing narratives with themes of mortality and fragility. These elements serve as a silent undercurrent in my work, shaping my long-term projects with an enduring pulse, where each photograph contributes its own depth, range, and beauty to the broader story.

Inspired by pioneers in documentary photography and influenced by philosophical inquiries into perception and the human condition, my approach merges sculptural depth with immersive storytelling. Through my lens, I aim to challenge perceptions and invite contemplation, encouraging viewers to confront the vulnerability and resilience that define our shared humanity.

Driven by a desire to evoke emotion and provoke thought, my work seeks to forge a connection between creator and observer. I invite viewers to journey alongside me—to engage with images that resonate universally, revealing the profound impact of photography in shaping our understanding of life’s impermanence.

©Tony Chirinos, Melany, from the project Scarred

©Tony Chirinos, Michael, from the project Scarred

©Tony Chirinos, William, from the project Scarred

©Tony Chirinos, Lauren, from the project Scarred

ES: Can you share a little about your path in photography? TC: My path in photography began in high school, when I realized I wanted to be an art photographer. I was fortunate to have a photography teacher, Susan Maguire, who encouraged me to take that desire seriously. That encouragement stayed with me throughout my life. My journey wasn’t a straight line. I studied photography at Miami Dade Community College and Florida International University before earning my MFA at Columbia University. Along the way, I developed a strong technical foundation, eventually working as a biomedical photographer and establishing the Medical Photography Department at Baptist Health Systems in 1989. That experience taught me to look closely, to be patient, and to understand the power of a photograph to reveal something we might otherwise overlook. But my deepest interest has always been in using photography to explore the human condition—our vulnerability, mortality, identity, and the things we carry with us through life. For more than four decades, I’ve photographed people, places, and traditions that speak to these concerns. Much of my work comes from my own experiences, my family history, and my ongoing search to understand where I come from and how memory shapes who we are. Teaching photography at Miami Dade College has also become an important part of my photographic journey. My students continually challenge me to look at photography differently and remind me why I fell in love with it in the first place. Receiving the Callanan Excellence in Teaching Award in 2019, which honors photography educators nominated by students or colleagues, affirms the work I continue doing in the classroom. Yet, at its core, what motivates me as both a teacher and an artist remains the same thing that drew me to photography as a young man: the desire to look more closely, to ask questions, and to make photographs that help me understand something about myself and the world around me.

ES: Did you have an influential photography mentor or teacher? What was their biggest impact on you as both an artist and a teacher? TC: Without a doubt, one of the most influential people in my life was Susan Maguire, my high school photography teacher. I was a young man who wanted to become an artist but didn’t really know what that meant or whether it was even possible. Susan introduced me to the work of great photographers through books and helped me understand that photography could be much more than making a beautiful picture. It could be a way of thinking, a way of telling stories, and a way of understanding the world. What I remember most, however, was her generosity and the faith she placed in me. When I finally managed to buy an enlarger but couldn’t afford a lens for it, she lent me one of hers every weekend. That might seem like a small gesture, but to me, it meant everything. She was helping me pursue something I could barely afford to dream about. Years later, when I published my first monograph, The Precipice, I dedicated the book to her. I wanted her to know that her encouragement had stayed with me all those years. I think Susan also shaped the kind of teacher I try to be today. I know what it feels like to be a young student with a passion but very little certainty about the future. I try to recognize that in my own students. Sometimes, what a student needs most is not another technical lesson but someone who believes in them and encourages them to keep going. I can teach students how to use a camera, understand light, and make stronger photographs. But I also hope to give them something Susan gave me: the confidence to believe that what they want to do with their lives is possible. I don’t think there is a greater gift a teacher can give a student.

ES: You have exhibited widely, published books and zines and won many prestigious awards in photography, including the Guggenheim Fellowship (congratulations), how do you share your experience and success as an artist with your students? TC: I think one of the most important things I can share with my students is that being an artist is not just about making photographs. It’s about commitment, curiosity, discipline, and being willing to pursue something even when the path isn’t always clear. I try to lead by example. I continue to make work, apply for grants, publish books, exhibit, and put myself in situations where I have to take risks and learn something new. I want my students to understand that you never stop being a student yourself. I also believe it’s important to show them that there are real opportunities to make a living in photography. That’s why I invite former students who are working in the field to speak to my classes. When my students meet people who once sat in the same classroom and are now working as photographers, artists, or creative professionals, they begin to see possibilities for themselves that they might not have considered. Although receiving the Guggenheim Fellowship was a pivotal moment in my career, I see that recognition as more than a personal accomplishment. It gives me an opportunity to encourage my students to take their own work seriously, believe in what they are doing, and understand that their voices matter. Ultimately, I want my students to leave my classroom with more than technical skills. I want them to develop the confidence to pursue their own ideas, the discipline to keep working, and the understanding that a meaningful life in photography is possible. If I can help even one student find the courage to follow that path, I feel I’ve done something worthwhile.

ES: What’s next for you as an artist? TC: I think what’s next for me is, in many ways, a continuation of what I’ve been doing throughout my life: following my curiosity and pursuing the questions that keep me up at night. I have several projects that I’m deeply committed to. One is What the Land Remembers , in which I’m documenting the transformation of Homestead, a place that has been part of my life for decades. I’m interested in what happens to our memories and our sense of belonging as the landscape around us changes. The project is personal, but I think it also speaks to something much larger about how we live and what we leave behind. I’m also working on Scarred , a project exploring the visible and invisible scars people carry. I’m photographing individuals and pairing their portraits with handwritten accounts of their experiences. I’m interested in the stories behind those scars, the things we carry with us, and the ways pain shapes who we become. I hope the project creates a space for empathy and reminds us that, despite our differences, we share more than we realize. I’m continuing to develop work that explores vulnerability, mortality, identity, and the human condition. These are subjects I keep returning to because I don’t think I’ve exhausted what they have to teach me. At this stage in my career, I also want to be more intentional about bringing my work into the world—seeking exhibition opportunities, placing my photographs in collections, continuing to publish (my next photobook will be published by L’Artiere), and connecting with people who might recognize something of their own experiences in my work. I’ve been making photographs for more than 40 years, and I still feel that I have so much to learn. I don’t know exactly where the work will take me, and I think that’s a good thing. If I knew all the answers before I started a project, there would be very little reason to make the photographs. For me, what’s next is to keep looking, keep asking questions, and remain open to the possibility that the next photograph might teach me something I didn’t know I was looking for.

©Tony Chirinos, from the project What the Land Remembers

©Tony Chirinos, from the project What the Land Remembers

©Tony Chirinos, from the project What the Land Remembers

©Tony Chirinos, from the project What the Land Remembers

©Tony Chirinos, from the project What the Land Remembers

ES: How do you help your students tap into curiosity and the creative process? TC: I actually don’t give my students traditional photography assignments where I tell them what to photograph. I believe they already have something incredibly valuable to work with: their own lives, their experiences, their families, their neighborhoods, and the things that interest or concern them. My job is to help them recognize the possibilities in what is already around them. I encourage them to be curious, to slow down, to look more carefully, and to ask themselves why something matters to them. Sometimes the most meaningful photographs come from subjects they’ve known their entire lives but have never really learned to see. Of course, I teach them the technical aspects of photography, visual literacy, and how to make decisions about light, composition, time, and perspective. We spend a great deal of time looking at photographs, discussing them, and participating in critiques. I want students to understand not only how to make a photograph, but also why they are making it. I think it’s important that students develop their own voices rather than simply learn to satisfy a teacher’s expectations. When they photograph something personal, something they genuinely care about, the work often becomes more honest and meaningful. They begin to discover things about themselves in the process. For me, teaching is less about giving students answers and more about helping them ask better questions. I want them to leave my classroom understanding that photography isn’t just about pointing a camera at something. It’s about learning to see, finding meaning in the world around them, and discovering what they have to say about it.

ES: What is the most meaningful part of your job? TC: The most meaningful part of my job is seeing my students grow into independent thinkers who have the confidence to find their own way, both as photographers and as individuals. I believe my responsibility as a teacher is to give students the tools they need to think for themselves, make their own decisions, and develop their own voices. At some point, the umbilical cord must be cut, and I believe that needs to happen sooner rather than later. My goal isn’t to create students who depend on me for answers. It’s to help them develop the confidence to ask their own questions, take risks, make mistakes, and learn from them. One of the greatest rewards is seeing former students build successful careers in photography and other creative fields. Carlos Goldman, who became the Director of Photography for Inter Miami CF, Arturo Alcala, who works as a fashion photographer, and Richard Ramos, an entrepreneur and co-owner of Cardinal Lab, are examples of former students who have gone on to establish themselves professionally in different ways. I’m proud of what they’ve accomplished, but what means the most to me is knowing that they have found their own paths. Their success reminds my current students that studying photography can lead to real opportunities, and that there isn’t just one way to build a meaningful career. Teaching has also taught me that I can’t measure my success by how much my students depend on me. I measure it by their ability to move forward without me. When a former student no longer needs my guidance, but still chooses to come back, share their experiences, or help the next generation, that’s incredibly rewarding. Ultimately, I hope my students leave my classroom with more than the ability to make good photographs. I want them to have the curiosity, discipline, and independence to navigate the world on their own terms. Watching them do that is probably the most meaningful part of being a teacher.

Student Work and Statements

©Brianna Acevedo

©Brianna Acevedo

©Brianna Acevedo

There is nothing more significant to a student than to have a mentor who inspires you to challenge the way you view and understand the world. For me, Tony Chirinos is that individual who not only supports me throughout my journey as a photographer, but constantly motivates me to achieve the highest caliber of work that I could produce. I have been lucky enough to have been under the tutelage of Tony for many years now, whose enthusiasm and high standards for art encourage me to continuously think critically of the world while feeding my ambition to create works of significance. Because of Tony, I came to view photography as a viable career path and was steered to pursue higher education, leading me to Pratt Institute where I was beyond equipped with the knowledge and technical skills needed to earn a BFA. Moreover, fueled by the strong community Tony has created and the vitality of his role as a professor, I plan to further my studies in hopes of becoming a professor myself. As I continue to learn and grow throughout my career, it is a true gift to know that I have a mentor that I can always rely on to help me navigate the complexities and challenges of being a photographer.

Brianna Acevedo

Website: www.briannaacevedophotography.com

Instagram: @photoswithbrianna

©Lorena Marrero

©Lorena Marrero

©Lorena Marrero

What to say about Tony Chirinos? He is certainly the most challenging professor I have ever had the pleasure of studying under. His passion is infectious, and always motivated me to do my best, not only in class, but in my personal life. He has an obvious passion for photography, yes, but his devotion to education is what sets him apart. His knowledge is an inspiration and a goal. The goal is not to photograph and think the way he does, the goal is to use the way we think to inspire our images and visual narratives. He adapts his teaching style to match each student’s preferred learning method, molding us to be the photographers we want to be. Although he does not sugarcoat things, his honesty is what has taught me the most about photography. He makes learning fun whilst always maintaining a deep respect for the craft. A master in his field, and still a humble and caring individual. Tony Chirinos is the model of what a true professor should be. I am a better photographer and a better person because I met him, and for that I am forever grateful.

Lorena Marrero IG: @lorenalmarrero

©Jaider Moreno

©Jaider Moreno

©Jaider Moreno

I first met Tony back in Fall of 2022; I didn’t know what to expect. I still remember the first day I met him, he showed me around the darkroom and that was it, I got bit by the photography bug. It was the beginning of many days in that darkroom, a place that I genuinely consider my sanctuary. Being a part of the photographic program at Miami Dade College Kendall has helped me grow not only as a photographer but also as person, and I have no other than Tony Chirinos to thank for that. His passion, respect and work ethic for photography and its practice is something I admire and work hard at to implement in my life. I try to be a sponge and absorb as much of his knowledge of photography and its history as I possibly can. One of the many things I admire about Tony is that he truly and deeply cares about his students and wants us to grow. When I first began taking photo classes with him, I was (and to a certain extent still am) a very shy person, but Tony saw something in me that I had not seen in myself. When he asked me to be President of the Photo Club at MDC Kendall, I was hesitant at first to say yes but seeing that Tony believed in me and saw that I had the potential to lead, it shifted something inside me, something that I’ve carried with me ever since then. That decision changed the trajectory of my life. Tony has not only been my professor and mentor; he’s also been like a father to me. It’s an honor and privilege to know him.

Jadier Moreno IG: @jaider.m

Tony Chirinos is a Venezuelan-born documentary-style artist based in Miami. His career spans over forty years, exploring the theme of mortality and fragility. Chirinos is a recipient of fellowships including the prestigious John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation (2023), The Green Space Miami Grant (2024), Callanan Excellence in Teaching Award (2019), the South Florida Cultural Consortium (2010), and the William Talbott Hillman Foundation grant (2021) to financially assist in the printing production of his first monograph, “The Precipice.” Mr. Chirinos holds a Master of Fine Arts from Columbia University (2003). Trained as a Bio-medical photographer in 1985 at Miami Children’s Hospital, he went on to create the Medical Photography department at Baptist Health Systems in 1989. His work has been exhibited nationally and internationally, including participation in the III Bronx Latin American Art Biennial. His photographic series have been featured in Dear Dave, The British Journal of Photography, The Washington Post, Photo Eye, Edge of Humanity Magazine, Slate, Daily Mail, Business Insider, and Fotofilmic, among others. Chirinos was among 100 photographers who participated in Review Santa Fe in 2012, 2018, and 2019. His work is included in the collections of Museum of Fine Arts Houston, University of Colorado at Boulder, Candela Collection, Cuban Heritage Collection, Light Work, Photographic Center Northwest, Center for Creative Photography at the University of Arizona, and Mount Sinai Medical Center, among others. Mr. Chirinos is a professor of photography at Miami Dade College since 2003. Website: www.tonychirinos.com IG: @chirinostony

article_text:
奈良美智、2027年秋にSFMOMAで大規模展を開催。約100点を通して創作世界の変遷をたどる

2027年秋に 奈良美智 の大規模回顧展が サンフランシスコ近代美術館 で開催される。北カリフォルニア初となる包括的な回顧展には、絵画や彫刻、写真など、代表作約100点が集結する。

サンフランシスコ近代美術館 （San Francisco Museum of Modern Art、以下SFMOMA）は、2027年秋に 奈良美智 の大規模回顧展を開催すると 発表した 。奈良の創作活動を包括的に紹介する回顧展としては、北カリフォルニアで初めてとなる。

キュレーションは、SFMOMA絵画・彫刻部門のアソシエイト・キュレーター、ナンシー・リムと、ロサンゼルスを拠点とする吉竹美香がゲストキュレーターとして担当する。戦後・現代日本美術を専門とする吉竹は、 ロサンゼルス・カウンティ美術館 （LACMA）の奈良美智回顧展（2021-2022）や、香港の M＋ で行われた 草間彌生 の大規模回顧展「Yayoi Kusama: 1945 to Now」（2022-2023）などを手がけてきた。

本展では、同館7階の展示室を会場に、絵画、ドローイング、彫刻、インスタレーション、サウンド、写真など約100点が集結する。目玉となるのは、今回が初の海外展示となる《Voyage of the Moon（Resting Moon）》（2006）だ。奈良のドローイング制作アトリエを思わせる小屋の屋根には、大きな月の顔がひと休みするかのように置かれている。幼い頃から夜空に魅了されてきた奈良の想像力が反映された作品で、2020〜2021年には東京・ 森美術館 で開催された「STARS展：現代美術のスターたち―日本から世界へ」でも展示された。

本展では、こうした幼少期の記憶に根ざした作品に加え、東日本大震災以降に見られる奈良の表現の変化にも光を当てる。

SFMOMAによると、2011年の震災と福島第一原発事故を経て、奈良の作品は内省的な性格をいっそう強めたという。幾重にも重なる絵の具の層や、にじむような筆致、何かを探し求めるような人物のまなざしが特徴的な絵画に加え、手作業の痕跡や不完全さが残る近年の彫刻などを通じて、奈良の創作世界の変遷をたどる。

article_text:
Arpita Singh , an Indian painter whose hallucinatory work fused allusions to real-world violence with uninterpretable dream imagery, died on Monday in New Delhi. She was 89, according to a report by the Tribune that cited confirmation from her husband, the artist Paramjit Singh.

Singh frequently switched her technique and way of working across her six-decade-long career, though she is today most well-known for hallucinatory figurative paintings that are steeped in Hindu lore and Indian history. In her most famous paintings, gods and laypeople appear to float through the air in landscapes that vaguely recall maps.

Devi Pistol Wali (1990), arguably her most widely discussed painting, features a shrouded woman with many arms, one of which holds a gun to a man holding a sword. The painting has typically been described as a response to violence against women in modern-day India, but Singh discouraged these interpretations, saying that current events “come into my painting like the way light comes as colour and breeze comes as movement,” as she put it in a 2025 Guardian interview .

She also tended to rebut the repeated description of her work as dreamlike, since she could control what went into her art. “Her paintings are not dreamworlds—they are real worlds of her own creation,” wrote Meara Sharma in an Artforum essay on Devi Pistol Wali . “In the worlds of her paintings, objects do not ‘float,’ because gravity does not exist.”

Singh was one of the most high-profile Indian contemporary artists, with the artist receiving the esteemed Padma Bhushan award in 1991. The Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in New Delhi organized a retrospective of her work in 2019.

But outside India, Singh was not widely known until 2025, when the Serpentine Galleries staged a survey of her work in London. “An admired artist in India, Arpita Singh rarely shows in America and that is our loss,” wrote critic John Yau in a 2017 Hyperallergic review of an exhibition at New York’s Talwar Gallery, one of the few exhibitions of her work staged outside India that is listed on her CV. (Talwar is currently staging another Singh show, on view through February 27.)

Singh did not seem entirely fazed by the recent international reception of her work, however. In her Guardian profile, she merely called the Serpentine exhibition “a prestigious thing for me.”

Arpita Singh was born in 1937 in West Bengal, India, and moved in 1946 to New Delhi. Partition, the violent cleaving of British India into a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim-majority Pakistan, happened the following year and shaped some of Singh’s early memories. She recalled standing on her balcony and observing as a man was killed below.

She went on to attend Delhi Polytechnic’s art school, from which she graduated in 1959. Her teachers included modernists such as Biren De and Sailoz Mookherjea, and her education brought her into contact with books on European modernism. She recalled gravitating toward Der Blaue Reiter, Wassily Kandinsky, Paul Klee, and Marc Chagall.

Though Singh found success relatively early on in her career, showing with the dealer Kekoo Gendhy, who had helped make S. H. Raza and M. F. Husain famous, she felt uncertain about her figurations, which were done in a faux naive style. During the 1970s and ’80s, she started working in abstraction, producing austere, largely colorless images formed entirely from dots and dashes. By the end of the ’80s, however, she had returned to figuration.

There are signs that Singh is gradually growing in prominence. In 2021, her work appeared in a blockbuster exhibition of abstractions by women at the Centre Pompidou in Paris and that year’s edition of the Gwangju Biennale in South Korea. The next year, she showed at the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, India’s top contemporary art exhibition.

What became obvious as Singh grew more internationally famous was that few others have produced work like hers, both when she started and now. “I control the law,” Singh once said, speaking of the worlds she creates in her art. “I’m the master.”

article_text:
Die Kunst der Woche in Basel, Berlin, Frankfurt am Main, Hamburg, London, Luxemburg, Osnabrück, Wien und Wolfsburg

Mariana Cook in Basel

Barack und Michelle Obama, Jasper Johns, Ruth Bader Ginsburg: Mariana Cook hat sie alle porträtiert. Dann wandte sich die US-amerikanische Fotografin Motiven zu, die noch deutlich mehr Geschichte mitbringen: Steinen. Elf Jahre lang reiste sie um die Welt, um Findlinge aufzuspüren, die einst von Gletschern an Orte verfrachtet wurden, an denen sie eigentlich nicht hingehören. Cook fotografiert die gewaltigen Felsbrocken wie eigenwillige Persönlichkeiten, mal einsam in der Landschaft, mal fast skulptural. Ihre 74 Schwarz-Weiß-Aufnahmen sind nun erstmals in der Kulturstiftung Basel H. Geiger zu sehen. Entstanden sind sie ganz analog, mit Mittelformatkamera und natürlichem Licht. Selbst die Abzüge fertigt Cook noch von Hand in der Dunkelkammer an.

Mariana Cook "Out Of Place - Out Of Time" , Kulturstiftung Basel H. Geiger, bis 14. Februar

Abschiedswochenende des PalaisPopulaire in Berlin

Was bleibt vom Mythos Berlin als Kunstmetropole? Und wer soll eigentlich noch die ganze Kunst bezahlen? Zum Abschied wird es im PalaisPopulaire noch einmal grundsätzlich. Unter dem Titel "MerciPalais" lädt das Haus am Wochenende zu zwei Tagen voller Kunst, Musik und Gespräche ein. Am Samstag diskutieren Till Fellrath, Antje Majewski und Moritz van Dülmen über die Zukunft der Berliner Kunstszene. Anschließend geht es mit Andreas Beitin, Christine Würfel-Stauss und Britta Färber ums Geld und die Frage, wie sich Kultur künftig finanzieren lässt. Beide Talks moderiert Monopol-Chefredakteurin Elke Buhr. Dazu gibt es Führungen, Poesie, Workshops und am Samstagabend Musik und ein DJ-Set.

"MerciPalais" , Palais Populaire, Berlin, 21. und 22. November

Gisèle Freund in Frankfurt am Main

Nazi-Aufmärsche in Frankfurt, Walter Benjamin in Paris, Frida Kahlo in Mexiko: Gisèle Freund war mit ihrer Kamera überall dort, wo Geschichte geschrieben wurde. Leider nicht immer freiwillig: Als Jüdin und Sozialistin musste sie 1933 aus Deutschland fliehen, später weiter nach Argentinien. Berühmt wurde sie mit ihren Porträts von Intellektuellen und Künstlern, doch Freund interessierte sich genauso für das Leben auf der Straße, für Armut und politische Proteste. Das Jüdische Museum Frankfurt packt nun 32 Archivboxen aus und zeigt neben bekannten Bildern auch fotografische Experimente, Briefe und persönliche Dokumente. Dabei geht es nicht zuletzt um die Frauen, die Freunds Leben und Karriere prägten: Freundinnen, Geliebte und Unterstützerinnen wie Adrienne Monnier, Victoria Ocampo und Simone de Beauvoir.

Gisèle Freund "Out Of the Box" , Jüdisches Museum Frankfurt, bis 25. April 2027

Medienkunst in Hamburg

Wenn man einem Werk der Medienkunst den Stecker zieht, wird es zappenduster. Auch insofern passt der Titel der aktuellen Ausstellung in der Hamburger Kunsthalle : "Unstable Media in the 21st Century". Der Titel der Ausstellung ist dem 1987 veröffentlichten Manifest einer Gruppe niederländischer Medienaktivisten entlehnt, die unter "instabilen Medien" all jene verstanden, die auf elektronischen Wellen und Frequenzen basieren.

Zu sehen sind Werke aus der ganzen Welt, von der Miniatur bis zur großformatigen Installation. Harun Farocki oder Pierre Huyghe sind unter den Künstlern, aber auch eine jüngere Generation um Fiona Tan, Omer Fast oder Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Letzterem sind gleich zwei große Räume gewidmet. Seine Arbeit "Primitive" (2009) erzählt eine Geistergeschichte aus dem Nordosten Thailands. Dort gibt es einen Ort, den man als Mann lieber nicht besuchen sollte, da man riskiert, von einem Witwen-Geist entführt und in ein fernes Land zu ihren übrigen Ehemännern gebracht zu werden.

Die in Indonesien geborene, in den Niederlanden arbeitende Künstlerin Fiona Tan begibt sich in ihrer Arbeit "Ascent" (2016) auf eine visuelle Reise zum japanischen Berg Fuji. Im Raum nebenan zeigt Harun Farocki in der Installation "Parallel I-IV" (2012–2014) ein faszinierendes visuelles Essay über die Möglichkeiten der Computeranimation. (dpa/Monopol)

"Unstable Media in the 21st Century" , Hamburger Kunsthalle, bis 2. Mai 2027

Tarek Atoui in London

Als die Turbinenhalle der Tate Modern in London noch wirklich die Turbinenhalle eines Kraftwerks war, muss es dort ziemlich laut gewesen sein. Man kann sich vorstellen, dass der Lärm der riesigen Maschinen tief durch das ganze Gebäude vibriert hat. Auch Tarek Atoui lässt nun mit seiner Installation zur Hyundai Commission das Gebäude zart erzittern. Doch die Klänge, die seine von der Decke hängenden Instrumente erzeugen, sind alles andere als Lärm. Atoui hat archaische, indigene Instrumente benutzt und baut zeitgleich Rückkopplungen mit dem, was gerade im Raum geschieht, in die computergesteuerte Abfolge der Klänge ein.

Trommeln und Blasinstrumente verschiedener Größe, mechanisch von großen Klöppeln geschlagen oder von Luft in Schwingung gebracht, kreieren eine Soundlandschaft, in der man sich verlieren möchte. Und sie erzeugt Gemeinschaft. Die Menschen lauschen stehend oder flanierend, versammeln sich zu kleinen Picknick-Formationen, Leute legen sich auf große Steine und schauen an die Decke und auf das Fadenkonstrukt, an dem die komplexe Installation hängt. Manchmal, bei tiefen Tönen, übertragen sich die Vibrationen auf den ganzen Körper, und es fühlt sich an, als wäre das ganze Gebäude ein Instrument.

"Hyundai Comission: Tarek Atoui" , Tate Modern, London, bis 11. April 2027

Luxembourg Art Week im Großherzogtum

Auch auf der Luxembourg Art Week feiert man das zweihundertjährige Jubiläum der Fotografie. Und so zieht sich das Thema Foto durch das Programm der 78 Aussteller aus 15 Ländern, die sich zur Messe in temporären Zelten auf dem Champ du Glacis versammeln. 26 von ihnen sind bei der Sektion "Focus Photo" dabei und integrieren Fotografie in ihre Präsentation. So zeigt die Galerie Lelong neben Werken von Kiki Smith und David Nash auch Fotografien von Andy Goldsworthy. Und bei der Galerie F. Hessler tritt ein historisches Ensemble von Alina Szapocznikow mit Fotografien von Su-Mei Tse in Dialog. Die Luxembourg Art Week ist aber nicht nur ein Event für den Kunsthandel, sondern will auch übergreifende kulturelle Strahlkraft entwickeln, mit Art Walks durch die Stadt und Performances im Casino, in der Philharmonie und im Mudam.

"Luxembourg Art Week" , Luxemburg, bis 22. November

Maskerade im Felix-Nussbaum-Haus

Bei James Ensor tragen selbst die Skelette Masken. Im frühen 20. Jahrhundert war die Verkleidung in der Kunst weit mehr als ein harmloser Spaß. Max Beckmann und Otto Dix nutzten Masken, um gesellschaftliche Rollenbilder aufs Korn zu nehmen. Für den Maler der Neuen Sachlichkeit Felix Nussbaum bekam das Motiv eine besonders bittere Bedeutung: Schon 1928 malte er sich mit Maske, 1943 griff er im Exil erneut darauf zurück. Da ging es längst auch um Tarnung, Bedrohung und die Angst, die eigene Identität zu verlieren. Das Felix-Nussbaum-Haus in Osnabrück versammelt nun Arbeiten von Nussbaum und 16 weiteren Künstlerinnen und Künstlern, darunter Hannah Höch, Karl Hofer und Emil Nolde. Die Ausstellung zeigt, wie sich hinter grotesken Gesichtern und Verkleidungen die politischen und gesellschaftlichen Umbrüche einer ganzen Epoche verbergen.

Felix Nussbaum "Maskeraden" , Museumsquartier Osnabrück (Felix-Nussbaum-Haus), 22. November bis 4. April 2027

Franz West in Wien

Die Frage nach der Verschränkung von Kunst und Leben wird in den Skulpturen und unkonventionellen Raumkonzepten von Franz West (1947–2012) immer wieder gestellt. Im kommenden Februar wäre der Österreicher 80 Jahre alt geworden – ein Anlass, den zwei Wiener Institutionen mit Ausstellungen feiern. In der Albertina dürfen Wests legendäre "Passstücke" nicht fehlen: Durch Tragen, Halten und Anlegen passen sich die prothesenartigen Gebilde den Körperformen an und geben dem Publikum die Möglichkeit, mit ihnen zu interagieren.

Im Wien Museum steht Franz Wests Heimatstadt im Fokus, die den Künstler gleichermaßen inspiriert und irritiert hat. West begriff die Stadt nicht nur als Bühne, sondern auch als Material. Von den Farbtönen der Nachkriegsfassaden über Anspielungen auf die Wiener Moderne bis hin zu ironischen Reflexen auf Freud, Wittgenstein oder die hermetische Wiener Kunstszene finden sich zahlreiche Spuren der Stadtgeschichte in seinem Werk.

Franz West "Die Revolution der Skulptur" , Albertina Modern, Wien, bis 29. März 2027; "Franz West und Wien" , Wien Museum, bis 2. Mai 2027

Aïcha Khorchid in Wolfsburg

Aïcha Khorchids Menschenfiguren starren oft geradeaus, als suchten sie den Augenkontakt mit den Betrachtenden. Ob sie ihn finden, bleibt fraglich, die Figuren wirken traumverloren oder in Melancholie gefangen. Geradezu in Raster eingepfercht und an den Bildrand gedrückt wirkt die Figur in "Le jour de ménage". Die Frau, die nicht weiß, ob sie zuerst essen oder putzen soll, könnte Khorchid selbst sein. Erst vor sechs Jahren soll die Autodidaktin zu malen begonnen haben. Erstaunlich. Ihre Bilder sind formal erfindungsreich wie koloristisch ausgefeilt und haben einen ganz spezifischen Klang.

Eine Badewanne voll Blut, in das gespenstisch ein kreideweißer Duschvorhang hineinragt: In einem ihrer autobiografischen Bilder erzählt Khorchid vom Suizid ihrer Mutter, die von der 14-Jährigen nach der Schule tot aufgefunden wurde. In anderen Gemälden erinnert sich die Künstlerin an das Waisenhaus, in dem sie unterkam, oder an die Pflegeeltern in der Normandie, bei denen sich die Künstlerin nie wirklich zu Hause fühlte.

Khorchid war Model in Paris, Tänzerin in der Karibik, sie arbeitete als Dekorateurin, Choreografin und Schauspielerin. Mit 27 eröffnete sie auf Mallorca ein Mode- und Dekorationsgeschäft. Die Baleareninsel ist seither Khorchids Lebensmittelpunkt. Ihre erste Ausstellung liegt gerade einmal zwei Jahre zurück – die Gruppenschau "The Beauty of Diversity" in der Albertina Modern in Wien. Im Kunstmuseum Wolfsburg folgt nun die erste institutionelle Soloschau der Künstlerin.

article_text:
As flights across the U.S. came to a halt Friday amid a rare nationwide ground stop , President Donald Trump was in a meeting with actor Jon Voight to talk about jumpstarting support for a federal film incentive .

Voight and his team, Steven Paul and Scott Karol, were at the White House to urge the president to push for the film incentive during the lame duck session of Congress.

“It was exciting to watch,” Karol told Variety , saying the president was getting updates on the flight situation and also the capsized boat in New Orleans. “He’s concerned with different things because he’s the president. He gave us attention while taking care of two emergencies.”

Taylor Swift, Jaafar Jackson, ‘The Odyssey’ Among Hollywood Music in Media Awards Winners

Voight made an impassioned speech in support of the Hollywood tax incentive bill, which would provide a 20%-30% rebate on domestic labor costs for films and TV shows.

“He was telling (Trump) he has a helpful heart and he feels this can get done,” Paul said. Voight “was great. He was crying by the end of the meeting. It was an Academy Award-winning speech.”

While Voight was still in the room, the president sent out a Truth Social post reaffirming his support for the federal incentive and urging Congress to pass it.

“Meetings are being set up, routinely, with the Leaders of both Parties in order to, GET THIS DONE!” Trump wrote. “It is a very Bipartisan undertaking, especially in that so much of the money being lost to other countries is coming out of the Blue States. Hopefully Republicans and Democrats will get together and finalize this already very actively negotiated Legislation.”

He also noted that he was working with Sen. Adam Schiff — “believe it or not.” Karol said the team had met with Schiff earlier in the day, and Schiff told them to tell Trump: “This is Tim Scott’s bill and I’m there to help.”

Schiff responded to Trump’s post on X, saying that the bill should not wait until the Democrats take over in January.

“President Trump and I agree: it’s time for Congress to pass a federal film incentive,” Schiff wrote.

Rep. Laura Friedman, a Democratic co-author, also responded, saying “there’s no excuse to wait.”

“A national film and TV incentive means jobs in California, Georgia, New York, New Jersey and every state across the country,” she wrote. “Let’s get it done.”

Karol said that the challenge is finding a legislative vehicle, in which to include the incentive bill. He said that momentum has not slowed since the Republicans’ defeat in last week’s midterm elections.

“There’s good energy on both sides,” he said. “There’s no indication from either side of the aisle that this is something that is not as important as it was before the election.”

Earlier on Friday, Politico published an article saying “Hollywood’s tax credit push runs into a post-midterm wall.” The story quoted Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., as saying chances were “pretty low” of passing any tax bill during the lame duck session.

Supporters of the incentive hope that Trump’s post will encourage lawmakers to make it a priority. Voight has served as Trump’s ambassador to Hollywood, and has met with the president several times to encourage him to back the tax credit. Those meetings paid off in August, when the president first endorsed the measure, leading to the introduction of the bill on a bipartisan basis in September.

Trump’s comment on the film incentive preceded any public statement on the nationwide ground stop. Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of Homeland Security, did address the public after the ground stop was called, telling the nation, “This isn’t another 9/11. This is a telecommunication outage.”

Read Trump’s Truth Social post below:

“I am working with Senator Tim Scott and, believe it or not, Senator Adam Schiff, and, additionally, Senators John Cornyn, Raphael Warnock, Steve Daines, Bernie Moreno, Tim Sheehy, Alex Padilla, Mark Warner, Thom Tillis, Chris Coons, Katie Britt, and Dick Durbin, together with Representatives Jason Smith, Nathaniel Moran, Brian Jack, Linda Sanchez, and many others, both Republican and Democrat, on the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act. The support and popularity of doing this, and bringing Entertainment back to the United States of America, has been unbelievable! Hollywood, and so many other places, have been virtually ’emptied out’ by the Tax Incentives, and much more, given by other Countries. Everyone feels strongly about the Motion Picture and Television Industry — and so do I, and we all want to save it. It was MADE IN AMERICA, and must STAY IN AMERICA. The Entertainment Industry has largely moved to Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and other countries, but the actors, producers, and all others involved want to come back home! Importantly, hundreds of thousands of Blue Collar Workers will be positively affected, BIG TIME, by the passage of this Bill. The amount of money spent on these Tax Incentives will be made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury’s coffers. Meetings are being set up, routinely, with the Leaders of both Parties in order to, GET THIS DONE! It is a very Bipartisan undertaking, especially in that so much of the money being lost to other countries is coming out of the Blue States. Hopefully Republicans and Democrats will get together and finalize this already very actively negotiated Legislation. It can be done quickly, accurately, efficiently and, importantly, will benefit all of America. MAKE OUR ENTERTAINMENT INDUSTRY GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP”

Updated with remarks from Karol and Paul.

article_text:
Internazionale and Milan have unveiled plans for their new Generali Stadium, which will replace the shared San Siro venue from the 2031-32 season.

The stadium, sponsored by Generali – Italy’s largest insurance company – will have a capacity of 71,500 seats and is expected to cost the two clubs €1.2 billion (£1bn). The plans were revealed at a gala event at Milan’s Castello Sforzesco on Thursday – but some fans in attendance voiced their opposition to San Siro being demolished.

Shortly before the briefing began, a group of Inter fans walked into the courtyard of the castle and unfurled a banner reading “you will never extinguish the lights at San Siro,” and chanting “hands off San Siro.” Work on the new stadium is set to begin in 2028, on the site of the existing 75,000-capacity venue.

The Generali Stadium will be shaped “low in the body, and rises up at either end” behind the goals, architect Norman Foster said. David Manica, a stadium specialist who collaborated with Foster on the project, added that the steep-sided design aims to bring fans as close to the pitch as possible.

“The most important thing that we realised when we designed this project is that San Siro is a feeling,” Manica said. “It’s more than a building, it’s a feeling … we brought all the seats as close as possible to the field. They could not be any closer, it’ll actually feel as though you’re sitting on the grass.”

The stadium will also be capable of hosting NFL international games, rugby matches and concerts. Milan and Inter paid €197 million (£165m) to acquire the current San Siro stadium and its adjacent parking arenas. The current ground will be largely demolished once construction work nears completion.

Also known as the Giuseppe Meazza Stadium, San Siro opened in 1926 and is the largest sports stadium in Italy. It is considered to be one of European football’s most iconic venues, but requires extensive modernisation despite undergoing a number of renovations during its lifespan.

after newsletter promotion

The Generali Stadium could be used as a venue for Euro 2032, which is being jointly hosted by Italy and Turkey. Foster and Manica previously worked together on the new Wembley Stadium, while the architect’s Foster + Partners firm also designed the plans for Manchester United’s proposed new 100,000-capacity home.

article_text:
The American French Film Festival , which celebrated its 30th anniversary this year, has been on a journey to cultivate a new generation of French movie lovers for two decades with its educational program for Los Angeles high school students.

This milestone edition brought around 3,000 students to the DGA theater for five packed screenings of “In Waves,” Phuong Mai Nguyen’s heart-wrenching animated feature which was bought Netflix at Cannes.

Related Stories

Serielizados Takeaways: From HBO Max-3CAT New Show ‘The Orphans’ to ‘This is Not Finland,’ Catalonia Shows the Way to Quality Content and Partnerships

Adapted from AJ Dungo’s graphic novel at set in Southern California, “In Waves” is a love story between a shy teenage boy and the girl who teaches him how to surf and how to live, before she succumbs to cancer.

The screenings, which drew applause and tears throughout, also gave students the opportunity to engage in the post-screening Q&A with the film’s producer, Priscilla Bertin , and screenwriter Fanny Burdino.

Spearheaded by Anouchka Van Riel , the festival deputy director, the program brings together more than 60 schools over five days, with roughly half coming from the public school system and half from private institutions. It also reaches beyond French-language classes to students studying performing arts and other creative disciplines.

In an interview with Variety , Van Riel discussed the importance of the programme to allow younger audiences to discover international cinema at a time when arthouse moviegoers are aging and foreign-language films face growing challenges in U.S. theaters. She also talked about the program’s rapid growth, why subtitles are no longer the barrier they once were, and the powerful response to “In Waves” which Netflix is positioning in the Awards race.

How many students and schools participate in the program?

We have more than 60 schools participating over five days, so that’s more than 12 schools a day. We organize five screenings of the same film, each with around 600 students. That’s approximately 3,000 students every year. I’ve built a database of around 300 schools, and we start reaching out in May. Within a week of sending the first email, half the seats — around 1,500 — are already booked. Then I spend the summer filling the remaining places. There’s enormous demand. We also make a point of having a mix of public and private schools, roughly 50/50. That’s very important to us. For public schools, transportation can be a challenge. Some have to apply for grants just to pay for the buses. There’s an entire economy around organizing these trips, and a lot depends on the teachers.

How does the festival work with teachers to prepare students for the screenings?

We work with the American Association of Teachers of French, which prepares two educational guides, one in French and one in English. The French-language guide is around 100 pages long. It’s incredibly detailed and allows teachers to explore the film from multiple perspectives, including its themes and cinematic language. The guides are designed to help students study the film before or after the screening. And we don’t just work with French-language classes. Around half of the participating classes are English-speaking. Many Los Angeles high schools have performing arts programs, and those students come because they’re interested in cinema and want to meet the filmmakers. The majority of these kids have never attended a film screening followed by a Q&A. That’s something we want to change.

That’s surprising in Los Angeles, where the film industry is everywhere.

It’s extraordinary. I’m a member of the Producers Guild, and I receive invitations to screenings and conversations with filmmakers almost every day. There are incredible events happening constantly, but these kids don’t have access to them. Of course, if their parents work in the industry, that’s different. But otherwise, most students aren’t exposed to that world. I grew up in a small town in Alsace, and I remember my French teacher taking us to the movies all the time when I was in middle school. Some of those screenings even had Q&As. There’s a tradition of that in France that doesn’t really exist here in the same way. We used to organize masterclasses for university students, including at USC, but we realized it was difficult to attract them. They’re already surrounded by so many opportunities on campus. With high school students, we can work directly through the teachers. That’s how we’ve developed this program.

Is the goal ultimately to cultivate a younger audience for French cinema?

Absolutely. It’s about renewing the audience. A couple of years ago, we screened “The Marching Band,” and when the film was eventually released theatrically in the U.S., I was invited to moderate a Q&A. I loved the film, so I was very happy to do it. But the theater was only half full, and I don’t think there was a single person under 65. That’s the problem. Foreign-language films have traditionally been considered niche in the U.S. Streaming platforms have helped change that perception somewhat, but we still need to familiarize younger audiences with these films. That’s why this program is so important.

Are subtitles still an obstacle for younger American audiences?

Not nearly as much as people think. We’ve conducted surveys with students after the screenings, and more than 80% say subtitles aren’t a barrier to watching foreign-language films. It’s not a completely scientific study, but it gives us a good indication of how attitudes are changing. Between streaming platforms, social media and series like “Squid Game,” young people have become accustomed to watching subtitled content. Sometimes there’s still a little hesitation before the screening. But once they’re sitting in the theater, they realize it’s easy. I really don’t think subtitles are the problem for this generation anymore. Distribution is a major part of the problem. That’s why streaming platforms have become so important for the circulation of foreign-language films. But there’s also the question of exposure. If young people aren’t given opportunities to discover these films, they’re not necessarily going to seek them out themselves.

This year’s selection was “In Waves.” What made it particularly suitable for the program?

There’s a wonderful connection between this film and the festival. The producer, Priscilla Bertin, had already come to the festival two years ago with “Wild Diamond,” and at the time she was in post-production on “In Waves.” We became familiar with the project very early, and it made complete sense for us to bring it back this year. What’s interesting is that the film is based on an American graphic novel that was discovered by a French producer in a secondhand bookstore in France and developed into a movie. We explain that background to the students before the screenings, including why it’s considered a French film and the response has been extraordinary.

The screenings were packed, and the students seemed particularly moved by the film. What was the atmosphere like?

It was very striking. At the first screening, I went straight into introducing the filmmakers for the Q&A, and I realized something wasn’t right because the students were still processing what they’d just watched. Usually, when a film ends, the students immediately line up to ask questions. But with “In Waves,” it took time. Every day, there was this moment of silence. The film had affected them so deeply that they needed a little time before they could speak. There’s something cathartic about sitting in a dark theater with other people, crying together and sharing the same emotions. You feel safe because everyone is experiencing that grief together. I think young people have fewer opportunities to experience cinema that way now. That’s what made these screenings so special.

article_text:
T hough it is my personal opinion that Christmas should not begin until after Thanksgiving, I am pleased to say that we already have at least one treat in Netflix’s holiday movie assembly line: Guarding Stars, starring Leighton Meester as a frosty bodyguard tasked with protecting Jared Padalecki’s movie star at, of all places, his family’s Montana ranch, falls on the fizzy side of seasonal fluff.

Good holiday movies are an exercise in knowing silliness, and so it is a relief when the first 10 minutes of this movie, directed by Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum, strikes the rare December balance between hearth-like warmth (the twinkle in Meester’s chocolate eyes when her Hannah Brooks lands a verbal punch) and complete lunacy (she lands that punch in an argument with her ex about … cuddling … literally seconds after thwarting an assassination attempt in Times Square). As a homespun band of hot would-be cowboys later drawl at a Christmas parade in “Montana” (Canada, per usual): “Christmas is back, y’all.”

So is Meester: the actor still best known for playing the Upper East Side’s ultimate ice queen in Gossip Girl is one of the few who can pull off “career woman with a heart of stone” with enough zest to overpower cliche. One believes, even accepts, when Meester’s Hannah, dressed in FBI office drag and glasses almost campy in their unsexiness, refuses both hugs and the suggestion of paid rest following the death of her mother, instead opting for the assignment in Montana because she feels “constantly overlooked and underestimated, nobody sees me coming”.

Guarding Stars, adapted from Katherine Center’s novel by Erin Cardillo and Richard Keith, is so named for the unenviable – at least, to the no-nonsense Hannah – task of protecting celebrities as opposed to, say, defusing IEDs in Afghanistan. Is it ever plausible that Meester, forever shaded with peak millennial resting bitch face, toted an assault rifle in the Middle East (as doctored pics helpfully suggest)? Absolutely not, but Meester is an amiable and capable salesman of a woman perpetually unimpressed, particularly when she jiujitsus a skeptical Jack Stapleton (Padalecki) to the ground.

As an action movie star akin, as best as I can tell, to John Krasinski-as-Jack Ryan, Padalecki is perfectly suitable – grizzled, wearing aviator sunglasses, voice 20% huskier than usual and just the faintest whiff of the narcissism of a real People’s Sexiest Man Alive. There’s an immediate spark to the two leads – one a fake action hero, the other too vigilant for her own good, both lonely. But it is mostly a testament to Meester’s sparkling intelligence – you know she knows what’s up – that one happily glosses over 1. Why Jack needs a bodyguard (a stalker, I guess?) and 2. Why Jack immediately insists that his bodyguard also plays his fake girlfriend for Christmas (mom has cancer).

No matter! Hannah promptly gets a makeover straight out of the Sundance catalog (somehow, not one of the movie’s many clear brand sponsors) and bunkers down at the ranch with Jack’s ailing mother (Andie MacDowell, bringing the movie equivalent of simmering homemade stew), gruff father (Shaun Johnston), wary brother (Noah LaLonde) and rodeo queen sister-in-law (Siobhan Williams). Also, a handful of kids and some horses, all creatures that lone-wolf Hannah would ordinarily neutralize in less than two minutes. Meester/Hannah instead make slow, steady inroads on the verboten realm of “the personal” with enough sincerity and self-awareness to puncture one’s perhaps military-grade sap defenses. (That the obligatory grief/trauma reveal hits harder than expected – which is to say, it hits at all – is thanks largely to the savvy use of camcorder footage, an instant nostalgia trapdoor for this film’s core audience of elder millennials.)

It’s not that Guarding Stars is tinkering much with the recipe; it checks the same boxes and clears the same hurdles as any other holiday romcom – mollifying snowball fight, awkward “fake” kiss, unconvinced family, late-stage family blow-up and romantic revelations – but with the swiftness and action sequence flourishes of a professional athlete. Or, perhaps more accurately, an ex-army bodyguard adept at the tuck and roll. Female hyper-competence, it turns out, pairs well with holiday cheer, and when it’s Meester once again taking no prisoners, you have my attention.

Netflix

Andie MacDowell

article_text:
Born in 1987 and based in Gunma Prefecture, Japan, Mari Katayama makes self-portraits, hand-sewn objects and soft sculptures in which her own body sits alongside the things she assembles. She always presses the shutter herself, and she favors materials available to everyone, convinced that needle and thread are the strongest tools. Her work questions assumptions about what is natural, artificial or expected of a body. In 2022, Tate acquired her self-portrait “bystander #23” (2016), which went on view at Tate Modern the following year.

This video is a short documentary produced by Tate, “Art should be for everyone.” Katayama describes her creative process, her need for a quiet place to work, and why, in her view, art belongs to everyone, whatever materials are used.

10 minutes, in Japanese with English subtitles.

Video © Tate. More information on Mari Katayama here.

article_text:
Die Kunst der Woche in Berlin, Karlsruhe, Hamburg, London, München und Paris

Susan Hiller in Berlin

Was passiert, wenn man lange genug auf einen flackernden Fernsehbildschirm starrt? Vielleicht sieht man irgendwann Geister. In den 1980er-Jahren kursierten tatsächlich Berichte über gespenstische Erscheinungen auf TV-Geräten nach Sendeschluss. Für die Künstlerin Susan Hiller war das ein gefundenes Fressen: Sie machte den Fernseher zum modernen Kaminfeuer, vor dem sich allerlei Fantasien entfalten. Überhaupt hatte die 2019 verstorbene Britin eine Schwäche für alles, was sich einer vernünftigen Erklärung entzieht: UFOs, Nahtoderfahrungen, Spukgeschichten und Menschen, die angeblich schweben können. "Ich habe mich der Arbeit mit 'Geistern' verschrieben", sagte sie einmal.

In ihrer ersten Berliner Überblicksausstellung "Bad Dreams" bei KW begegnet man nun einer Wand aus alten Röhrenfernsehern, aus denen Menschen von Begegnungen mit dem Jenseits erzählen, Fotografien scheinbar schwereloser Körper und Kindern mit übernatürlichen Fähigkeiten. Ob das alles wirklich passiert ist, interessierte Hiller weniger als die Frage, warum wir solche Geschichten erzählen und so gern an das Unheimliche glauben. Außerdem eröffnen die Ausstellungen "Ousssean" der südkoreanischen Künstlerin Koo Jeong A sowie Rafik Greiss' "The City and the City".

Susan Hiller "Bad Dreams" , Koo Jeong A "Ousssean" , Rafik Greiss "The City and the City" , KW Institute of Contemporary Art, Berlin, 17. Oktober bis 10. Januar 2027

Contemporary African Art Fair in London

Parallel zur Frieze kommt an diesem Wochenende die 1-54 Contemporary Art Fair für Kunst aus Afrika und der afrikanischen Diaspora zum 14. Mal nach London – mit einer Neuerung: Als Reaktion auf das wachsende Interesse am afrikanischen Modernismus widmet die Messe im Somerset House der Kunst der Moderne einen eigenen Schwerpunkt. Kuratierte Messekojen präsentieren Meister des 20. Jahrhunderts wie Seyni Awa Camara aus dem Senegal, Aubrey Williams aus Guyana, Tahia Halim aus Ägypten und Twins Seven Seven aus Nigeria.

Ergänzt wird der Schwerpunkt durch die von der Kunsthistorikerin Nancy Dantas kuratierte Gruppenausstellung "West Wind". Ein weiterer Fokus liegt auf Künstlerinnen: Die Londoner Gillian Jason Gallery und O’DA Art aus Lagos widmen ihre Präsentationen ausschließlich weiblichen Kunstschaffenden.

"1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair" , London, bis 18. Oktober

Open Art in München

Die Open Art Munich zählt zu den traditionsreichsten Veranstaltungen ihrer Art: Seit 1989 laden die Münchner Galerien zum Saisonstart im Herbst zu einem gemeinsamen Ausstellungswochenende ein. In diesem Jahr findet es im Oktober parallel zur Messe Munich Highlights statt. An diesem Wochenende öffnen rund 50 Galerien ihre Türen und laden zum Rundgang ein. Bei Walter Storms präsentiert der konzeptionelle Bildhauer und Objektkünstler Gerold Miller neue Werkgruppen in drei Galerieräumen. In der Galerie Klüser erkunden Lori Nix und Isca Greenfield-Sanders mit fotografischen und malerischen Arbeiten die instabile Konstruktion von Wirklichkeit. Ein Highlight im Bereich der jungen Kunst ist die Ausstellung von Sophia Mainka in der Galerie The Tiger Room.

Open Art Munich , München, bis 18. Oktober

Neues Museum Large in Paris

Begrünte Terrassen, Uferpromenaden und ein elegantes Gebäude, in dessen Kupferfassade das Sonnenlicht spielt: Man muss die Augen schon sehr eng zusammenkneifen, um sich auszumalen, dass die Île Seguin bei Paris vor nicht allzu langer Zeit noch ein gigantischer Industriestandort war. Fast 70 Jahre lang betrieb der Autobauer Renault auf der Seine-Insel eine der größten und modernsten Fabriken der Welt. Nach der Schließung und dem Abriss der Gebäude im Jahr 2005 wollte sich Luxusmogul François Pinault hier ein Privatmuseum von Tadao Ando bauen lassen – er scheiterte an der Bürokratie.

Vier Jahre später wurde der Architekt Jean Nouvel mit dem Masterplan für ein Kulturquartier beauftragt. Der erste Meilenstein war ein Musikzentrum, der zweite folgt ab Samstag mit der Eröffnung eines Zentrums für zeitgenössische Kunst namens Large. Der von RCR Arquitectes (Pritzker-Preis 2017) entworfene Bau umfasst 5000 Quadratmeter. Die von Cecilia Alemani kuratierte Auftaktschau "Moteur Imaginaire" beleuchtet die Verbindungen zwischen Mensch und Maschine. In Zusammenarbeit mit dem Renault-Fonds für Kunst und Kultur stellt sie historische Meisterwerke von Vasarely, Dubuffet, Tinguely und Doisneau in einen Dialog mit 17 Auftragsarbeiten zeitgenössischer Künstler wie Théo Mercier, Sara Sadik oder Bertrand Lavier.

"Imaginary Engine" , Large – Zentrum für zeitgenössische Kunst Île Seguin, Paris, 17. Oktober bis 7. März 2027

Fake News in Hamburg

Wie sich Nachrichten in Zeiten von Desinformation, künstlicher Intelligenz und sozialen Medien verändern, zeigt eine neue Ausstellung im Hamburger Museum der Arbeit. Die Schau " Nachrichten – News" beleuchte dabei nicht nur die Geschichte der Nachrichten , sondern auch die Arbeit der Menschen, die hinter den Nachrichten stehen, sagte Kuratorin Sandra Schürmann. Beide Perspektiven würden eingenommen: die der Nachrichtenproduzenten und der Nachrichtenkonsumenten.

Vor dem Hintergrund eines schwindenden Vertrauens in die Medien behandele die Ausstellung "topaktuelle Themen", sagte Museumsdirektorin Rita Müller. "Es geht um den Umgang mit Informationen, mit Nachrichten , es geht um Desinformation, Fake News, Glaubwürdigkeit, Vertrauen, es geht um Pressefreiheit und schließlich geht es auch um unsere Demokratie."

Besuchern wird ein Blick hinter die Kulissen verschiedener Medien und die Arbeit von Agenturen, Korrespondenten und Redaktionen geboten. Die interaktiven und multimedialen Angebote richten sich an alle Altersgruppen ab der neunten Klasse.

"Nachrichten – News" , Museum der Arbeit, Hamburg, bis 16. Mai 2027

Mars-Performance in Karlsruhe

Tütennahrung, Konservenfutter, manchmal auch frittierte Insekten und das Ganze unter ständiger Beobachtung durch Passanten – auf dem Karlsruher Marktplatz startet eine Marsmission der besonderen Art. In eine extra dafür aufgebaute und mit einer weißen Plane bedeckte Metallkuppel ziehen Künstlerinnen, Künstler und Mitarbeiter des Zentrums für Kunst und Medien (ZKM) ein und simulieren darin in einer Art Dauerperformance das Leben auf einer Marsstation.

Immer drei Personen in wechselnder Besetzung sollen dabei im "Red Dust City" genannten Habitat bestimmte Aufgaben erfüllen und etwa erforschen, wie sich Zusammenleben gestalten lässt, wie man mit Ressourcen wie Wasser umgeht oder wie man nachhaltig leben kann. Interessierte oder zufällig vorbeilaufende Passanten können die ZKM-Crew durch ein etwa zwei Meter großes Guckloch-Fenster beobachten oder durch eine transparente Tür hereinschauen, wie ein ZKM-Sprecher erläuterte. Wie die Crew schläft, sich wäscht oder auf die Toilette geht, sei neugierigen Blicken aber entzogen.

Die Ergebnisse der mehrtägigen Aktion seien natürlich nicht für eine mögliche spätere Besiedelung des Mars gedacht. Sondern sie dienten dazu, den Blick auf den Umgang der Menschen mit der Erde zu lenken, die zunehmend unbewohnbar werde, hieß es weiter. Nach einem streng getakteten Zeitplan heißt es für das jeweils in der Kuppel wohnende Trio dann Tag für Tag: Frühstück, Forschung, Bewegung und Mittagessen, Forschung, Abendessen und ins Bett gehen. Für sogenannte Außeneinsätze darf die Crew die Kuppel manchmal auch verlassen – und wird sich dann ohne Kontakt zu den Passanten drumherum in Astronautenanzügen über den Marktplatz bewegen. (dpa)

"MARS!-Performance" , Aktion des ZKM – Zentrum für Kunst und Medien Karlsruhe auf dem Karlsruher Marktplatz, bis 27. Oktober
