article_text:
On October 30 of last year, we lost one of cinema’s most daring auteurs: the British director Peter Watkins. Starting out in television in the 1960s, Watkins developed an utterly unique and militantly political mode of filmmaking. In works like Culloden (1964) , The War Game (1966) , Punishment Park (1971) , and his magnum opus, La Commune (Paris, 1871) (2000), he cast nonprofessional actors in enactments of political events from the past, present, or a dystopian future, which he then shot in the style of live news reporting on TV. The results are thrilling films that startle with their naturalism and urgency, and provoke thorny questions about authoritarianism—not just of the state, but also of the media.

To commemorate this great filmmaker’s legacy, Film Comment editor Devika Girish invited critic J. Hoberman, who has not only admired and written about Watkins’s work, but also took a class with the man himself back in the 1970s. They talk about the trajectory of Watkins’s life and work, what makes his films feel so singular even today, and the contemporary directors that carry forward his legacy.
excerpt_original: Living history: critic J. Hoberman joins to discuss the late British director’s utterly unique and invigoratingly political cinema

article_text:
The Hunger Games. Rocky Balboa. Godzilla. Ebenezer Scrooge. Cliff Booth?

November is chock full of IP hoping to secure massive Thanksgiving holiday receipts at the box office, but don’t let those familiar names shield your attention from the buzzy indies and Oscar hopefuls screening beside them.

This is the first big drop of award season goodies vying for any leg up they can muster as far as piquing Academy members’ interest. So, your ticket purchase means a lot more for the festival darlings than it does the board of directors of whichever shareholder-driven CEO is currently holding an Infinity Gauntlet of legacy studio cachet.

Maybe some of the below posters will sway you.

Together

Brandon Schaefer and Jump Cut start things off with the simple yet effective one-sheet for Soul Patrol (limited, November 6). It utilizes a great candid shot of the film’s subject: the Vietnam War’s first Black special ops team. The muted colors and grainy texture put the era on display while the demeanor of these men provides a promise for inspiration rather than tragedy.

From there the text falls in on the center y-axis to keep our eyes moving up and down vertically from laurels to quotes to titles to image and back again. The pop of red with the title isn’t overpowering thanks to a gradient fade into the gray sky and the unassuming sans serif of the whole ensures the men always remain our focus.

Did I sneak in a little IP next courtesy of AV Print’s Focker-in-Law (November 25)? Yes, but it’s a fun concept that keeps the ethos of the series alive without the need of any crazy swings. All that’s necessary is a quick shift of the frame.

Not only is cropping Ben Stiller out of the picture hilarious on its own, but it’s even funnier to see that he’s the only one trying to be in the photo in the first place. His one eye is looking directly at us while De Niro side-eyes Stiller and Grande side-eyes De Niro. It’s all about the franchise’s themes of mistrust and skepticism. Rather than tease that Greg might become Jack where his new future daughter-in-law is concerned, however, should we wonder if she’s the one judging whether the Fockers are worthy of her?

That ambiguity is what makes it noteworthy. The other layout with a lie detector scene? That just makes it seem like they’ve remade the first film.

From a group to a trio, we now move to a kinetic pair dancing in a bright, kaleidoscopic radial blur courtesy of George McWilliams (for GrandSon with photography by Ryan McGinley). Instead of just putting another glossy image on the wall, they deliver Club Kid (limited, November 6; wide, November 25) with a textured atmosphere that seeks to depict the scene’s energy more than its environment.

That’s why they push the text to the bottom. They don’t want to risk boxing in the rainbow of colors any more than the edges of the page do naturally. We’re supposed to feel the music. To imagine the entire poster pulsing to the beat like when you put sand on a speaker and watch it jump to the rhythm. It’s a gorgeous bit of sensory transference with sound being visualized as a warp speed burst flying past the central two men.

Drawn out

Tyler Rubenfeld goes literal with his hand-penciled poster for In the Mouth (limited, November 20). One man’s mustached lips open to hold the head of another man who subsequently holds the title in his. It’s like a Matryosha doll of faces. So much so that I’m surprised a third man (a smaller version of the first?) isn’t added to the chain rather than sat upon the second man’s shoulder.

The sheer lunacy is enough to turn heads, but the choice to go with black and white crosshatch amidst the usual slick photography of other posters guarantees it. Because even if you don’t notice the men from a distance due to the whole becoming a field of gray, the bright white of the title is unavoidable. The crisp edges render the letters into uncanny shapes so absent of color that they almost become mesmerizing tractor beams drawing us in closer.

Sam Smith’s Zi (limited, November 6) is drawn too, but with a computer rather than a pencil. Its outlined images look more like a map than a portrait as its vector line work overlap until its dual levels (black and red) merge to become one.

It’s a captivating image due to that flattening of perspective (despite the red image using perspective to mimic depth), but it’s a pitch-perfect calling card once you realize the thematic importance of this choice. Not to spoil anything, but Kogonada’s latest experimental feature plays with time in a way that allows its titular character to see her past and future selves in front of her depending on where and when she travels with in this city.

So, we’re talking about one drawing being projected on the other as much as a uniform coexistence between the two thanks to Smith’s wonderful decision to sometimes use both colors for a single line. They are simultaneously at odds and in concert. Dream and reality. Physical and illusion.

While Fourth Wall Studio’s poster for Birds of War (limited, November 4) isn’t fully illustrated like the previous two, its detailed drawings are exquisitely rendered to make you wonder if they should have left the two people below off the page completely.

That would be a mistake, though, considering this documentary is about them and the parallel lives they’ve lived over thirteen years of love, war, and exile. Their placement is therefore crucial to the whole because they become guardians of their two halves. The destruction in front of their camera lenses and the not quite symmetrical drawings above them of birds and bombs.

Two people. Two sides. One title treatment that merges the colors and motifs into a stunning block augmented by the red sun above and red tagline below. Black and white for detail. Red for color fields. Blue for a hopeful sky of possibility.

Boxed

While simple on its surface, Janie Stapleton’s Mouse (limited, November 6) packs a punch with that empty chair. This image is therefore as much about what we see as what we don’t. The weird depth of field reveals its probable Photoshop strings, but it too augments the fact that we’re supposed to be looking at both seats with equal importance. They pop out from the background—realistically or not.

I also just really like the balance of the text above and below the image frame. Everything at the top is shifted left. Everything at the bottom is shifted right. It’s a strong composition that gets to its point with purpose.

Jack Staniland’s (for CREATE) poster for Minotaur (limited, November 20) plays with its image box by repeating it six times for an effective conveyor belt effect that drags our vision through the page vertically from bottom to top. We’re stepping on rungs of a ladder as we rise from him to her (a new credit resting upon each separation) with a starkly brighter gap in-between showing a completely different scene of someone dragging a body outside. The latter is the perfect place to therefore situate the title on an island of its own.

You wouldn’t get that same motion had they just used the two images in full (one broken in half by the second). What would have been a stagnant triptych is now a subtly animated journey through emotional faces and uncertain fates.

Javier Jaén uses multiple image boxes for his Bitter Christmas (limited, November 13; wide, November 25) too. Rather than deconstruct and repeat an image, however, he turns this portrait into a collage of faces via multiple sets of eyes. It’s a stunning effect that causes us to imagine these six people all staring at the man whose image they cover. Think of the poster as a static representation of quick cuts around a dinner table at every guest revealing their current state of emotion. Or … are we seeing the different people who will look through that man’s eyes a la Being John Malkovich ?

That overload of potential information is why I think this is the best of the film’s three one-sheets. Jaén’s second optical illusion with a man’s silhouetted profile and a woman’s cropped portrait aligned off-center is a well-orchestrated visual, but it doesn’t have that same intrigue. Yes, you still get the notion of a blurred identity or focal point (the film tells two stories simultaneously), but it’s not nearly as evocative.

The same can be said for Andrew Bannister’s English-language iteration—although it’s a lot of fun, regardless. It uses color (blue and red) to denote the two narratives while also creating its own Matryoshka doll of cacti in cacti with a man’s head peeking out from inside too. The thorny foliage playing with the unusual use of “bitter” to describe a holiday generally synonymous with pleasure ties the whole together nicely.

title_original: Club Kid Review: A Bittersweet, Tremendously Moving Debut
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Cannes coverage. article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Cannes coverage. The film arrives in theaters on November 6.

It’s never wise to assume anything. Promotional materials doing the rounds before Club Kid ‘s raucous Cannes premiere this week suggested a New York downtown scene answer to Mia Hansen-Løve’s Eden , but Jordan Firstman’s funny, bittersweet, and tremendously moving directorial debut is as much a fresh reimagining of the stunted father subgenre that gave us everything from Kramer vs Kramer and Marriage Story to Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy . This is a movie that promises and delivers scenes of copious drug taking and gross-out comedy, but its third-act emotional payoff is as earned and devastating as the best of them.

For fans who’ve followed Firstman’s career from Rotting in the Sun to I Love LA , this duck-to-water move behind the camera will come as a welcome surprise. It’s notable that the movie opened in Un Certain Regard, a sidebar the festival’s programmers have often used as a testing ground for movie stars looking to try their hand at the tiller for the first time. The difference with Firstman’s confident arrival is that it feels less the work of a dilettante than a natural. Just look at Club Kid ‘s opening sequence, which opens on a fluid and immersive “oner” by cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra (who shot The Studio and The Last Black Man in San Francisco ) that takes us from the front seat of an Uber all the way onto the dancefloor of Club Labor, where Peter Green (Firstman) and his entourage are greeted like Henry Hill at the Copacobana. It’s 2016 and the party’s just getting started. But soon the movie wakes up in the present day, a few thousand mornings after the morning after—an alerting choice and the first glimmer of Club Kid ‘s larger ambitions.

The next comes a few scenes later with the abrupt arrival of an English lad named Arlo (Reggie Absolom), a ten-year-old from London who was conceived during a drug-fuelled moment between Peter and an English tourist on that fateful 2016 night. It’s here that Club Kid begins its unlikely journey into the lineage of those Hoffman and Sandler classics, becoming a story less about an aging party boy than a underqualified man coming face to face with the realities of fatherhood for the first time. Been-there, done-that? Perhaps. But no other movie in this subgenre has yet, to my knowledge, contained a scene in which father and son sing Ethel Cain in duet on piano, or the wisdom that fisting can be “lowkey spiritual,” or that a cocktail of G and alcohol is rarely (if ever) advisable.

Those moments and sharp-witted snatches of dialogue are just some of many things that make Club Kid such an engrossing and enjoyable watch—a movie with a clear sense of place and lived experience and packed to the brim with great music (Arthur Russell and Elliott Smith both feature) and personality. For the latter, there is Peter’s lively milieu, which boasts enough girls, gays, and theys to fill a movie twice this size. The movie of course revels in that world of joyful debauchery in its first half, which makes it doubly gratifying that, even after Arlo’s arrival and Peter’s inevitable decision to clean up his act, that the movie never once wags a finger at the life and people being left behind. When a bleary-eyed Peter tells his coked-up business partner Sophie (Cara Delevingne) that he’s turned to dealing drugs at the club partially to keep the community safe, there’s more than an ounce of truth to it—even if we know that, by the laws of screenwriting, those choices will inevitably come back to bite him. As with any well-worn genre piece, you’ll see story beats coming a mile away, but I welcomed their arrival with open arms.

Add to this a refreshing amount of real bustling streets and choice locations (a lunch scene at Balthazar here, a walk by the East River there, an always welcome shot of the city’s skyline from the window of a car at night) and you end up with one of the best (at least from this outsider’s perspective) New York movies of this scale since at least Past Lives . In a deceptively challenging lead role, Firstman locates an emotional register that feels perfectly in-step with his natural gifts as a comedic actor, and he’s backed by a supporting cast that includes Babylon ’s hunky Diego Calva as a love interest, Hollywood veteran Colleen Camp as an eccentric neighbor, and—naturally—a who’s-who of the downtown scene (keep an eye out for Nick Pinkerton). Delevingne can chew scenery a bit much for comfort and I probably could have done without Arlo’s DJ subplot (which, as Peter notes, is indeed “lowkey corny”) but Club Kid looks every inch the work of a mature, gifted filmmaker with plenty to say and the guts to lay it all out.

Club Kid premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.

article_text:
General information

Website

Entrance fee US$50

For additional questions, email to info@smithfund.org

Timeline

Call for entries open – 02 July 2024

Waiver Deadline – 24 September 2024

Submission deadline – 08 October 2024 at 11:59 pm EDT

Grant recipients announced – 10 December 2024

45th Annual W. Eugene Smith Grant Ceremony – TBD

The W. Eugene Smith Grant is designed to encourage and support visual storytellers whose photographic work renews the tradition of W. Eugene Smith’s dedicated compassion as evidenced during his 45-year career as a photographic essayist. Special consideration will be given to work that promotes social change, that embraces new technologies and image distribution, and that seeks to integrate the tradition of photography and social change with contemporary practice. The judges will be looking for a photographer and project that seem most likely to use exemplary and compelling photojournalism and documentary photography (possibly supplemented by or incorporating multi-media) to address an issue of import and impact related to the human condition: social change, humanitarian concern, armed conflict, or other topics of interpersonal, psychological, cultural, social, environmental, scientific, medical and/or political significance, ideally expressing an underlying acknowledgement of our common humanity.

For 2024, the amount of the W. Eugene Smith Grant is $30,000. In addition, two $10,000 Finalist Grant will be awarded

A fee waiver of US$50 will be granted to a selected number of photographers in Southeast Asia upon request sent to Matca via email at hello@matca.vn.

Heute etwas aus den Untiefen der sozialen Medien. In der letzten Woche hat ein Post des Instagram-Accounts @thewaronbeauty eine gewisse Aufregung bei einigen einschlägigen Kunstwelt-Instagrammern verursacht. Die selbsternannte "ästhetische Evangelistin" Julia James Davis führt seit über zwei Jahren einen Kreuzzug gegen die vorherrschende zeitgenössische Kunst, die ihrer Meinung nach "die Schönheit in all ihren Formen systematisch zerstört." Mit ihren MAGA-Tiraden hat sie immerhin mehr als 180.000 Follower zusammengebracht – Tendenz stark steigend.

Der Kunstszene war das bisher egal. Bis sie letzte Woche eine Ausstellung von Kiki Smith bei Jeffrey Deitch in Los Angeles besucht hat. Der dort vorgefundene "Kunstterrorismus" hat sie anscheinend so bis ins Mark erschüttert, dass sie noch am Tag darauf nur weinend vor die Kamera treten konnte, um in einem zehnminütigen Sermon das Verbot solcher Kunst und die Verhaftung der Beteiligten zu fordern. Das Ganze ist eine ziemlich abgeschmackte Show, aber eben auch genau das: eine Show.

Denn neben ihrem pseudoreligiösen hat Davis auch noch einen kommerziellen Auftrag. Ihre Firma Jay Day Dress Co. ist eines "der letzten verbliebenen familiengeführten Luxusmodehäuser in Amerika", so die Selbstdarstellung . Die Textilfirma, gegründet von ihrem Urgroßvater und in den 1950er-Jahren eingestellt, produziert heute genau ein Modell, das irgendwie nachhaltige "Promise Dress" für 709,95 Dollar. Ihr Kulturkampf-Gehabe ist reines Ragebait , um ihrer Anhängerschaft überteuerten religiösen Nippes-Schmuck zu verkaufen, den sie in reicher Auswahl in ihrem Webshop anbietet.

Und genau diesen Köder schlucken einige Betreiber von Instagram-Accounts aus der Kunstszene anscheinend nur zu gerne, etwa @carriescotcurates (68.000 Follower) oder @theartdaddy (18.000 Follower). Denn auch ihnen beschert ein Aufreger Reichweite. Während Carrie Scott eher Kunst einem größeren Publikum nahebringen will und auch schon mal zum Blutspenden aufruft, wendet sich Art Daddy gezielt an ein Szenepublikum.

Hinter dem Pseudonym verbirgt sich laut Kenny Schachter die Kunst- und Kulturwissenschaftlerin Anni Irish . Bekanntheit erlangte die Figur durch ihre oft sarkastische mediale Begleitung der Karrieren der Instagram-Persona Jerry Gogosian und ihrer in diesem Jahr verstorbenen Schöpferin Hilde Lynn-Helphenstein, des Richard-David Prechts der Kunstwelt, Magnus Resch, sowie des ehemaligen professionellen Pokerspielers und Musikproduzenten Jeff Magid, der als magideye zunächst bei Instagram und mittlerweile auch bei der Art Basel versucht, als Experte fürs Kunstsammeln durchzugehen. Sie weiß also, wie man mit Kontroversen Aufmerksamkeit erzeugt.

Futter für den Troll

Einen redlichen Versuch der Auseinandersetzung unternimmt der einige Tage darauf in die Diskussion eingestiegene Künstler und studierte Psychologe Gabriel Allred , der @waronbeauty akribisch rechtes Dogwhistling und Antisemitismus nachweist. Das ist ehrenwert, aber kontraproduktiv. Denn Scharlatane, die einem verblendeten Publikum mit ihrer Hetze irgendwelche Produkte andrehen wollen, leben von der Empörungsmaschine der sozialen Medien, der Präsident der USA vorneweg.

In den 1990er-Jahren, als das Internet noch überschaubar war und Diskussionen in Usenet-Foren stattfanden, galt der Leitsatz " Don't feed the troll" . Heute füttert man den Troll nur zu gerne, wenn er einem selbst Aufmerksamkeit beschert.

Davis stammt übrigens aus einer Milliardärsfamilie. Ihr Großvater Marvin hatte in den 1980er-Jahren das Filmstudio 20th Century Fox mit seinen Fernsehsendern an Rupert Murdoch verkauft. Ihr Vater Gregg ist ein Öl-Magnat. Der Lebensstil ihrer Familie soll als Inspiration für die Fernsehserie "Denver Clan" gedient haben. Und einer der Murdoch-Söhne hält mittlerweile bei der Art Basel das Heft in der Hand.

title_original: ウジェーヌ・ブーダン展　印象派の父 ― 光を求めて
editorial_title_zh: 尤金·布丹展：印象派之父——追寻光芒
editorial_excerpt_zh: 本展旨在介绍被称为“印象派先驱”与“印象派之父”的19世纪法国画家尤金·布丹（1824-1898）的艺术生涯。布丹以清新明快的色彩和轻快流畅的笔触表现故乡诺曼底的天空、海景以及牧场上的牛群而闻名。通过在户外直接观察自然，描绘瞬息万变的光线与大气，这种创作手法对包括年轻克劳德·莫奈在内的当时许多画家产生了巨大影响，并最终促成了印象派的诞生。View More > The post ウジェーヌ・ブーダン展 印象派の父 ― 光を求めて first appeared on ART iT（アートイット） .

article_text:
本展は、「印象派の先駆者」「印象派の父」と呼ばれる19世紀フランスの画家ウジェーヌ・ブーダン（1824-1898）の画業を紹介する展覧会です。ブーダンは故郷ノルマンディーの空、海景、牧場の牛などをみずみずしい色彩と軽快な筆運びで表現したことで知られます。戸外で自然をじかに観察しながら、うつろいやすい光や大気を描写する制作手法は、若きクロード・モネをはじめとする当時の画家たちに大きな影響を与え、やがて印象派の誕生につながっていきます。特に空や雲の表現は詩人ボードレールに「気象学的美の世界」と評され、バルビゾン派の画家コローに「空の王者」と称賛されています。 日本では30年ぶりの本格的な展覧会となる今回は、人物や建築モチーフなどにも焦点を当てつつ、油彩、素描、パステル、版画などの約100点の作品により近代風景画の発展に大きく寄与したブーダンの魅力を新たな視点で問い直します。

会期 ／2026年11月28日（土）− 2027年1月31日（日）

article_text:
国際芸術祭「あいち2028」の会期・会場が決定。半田市と名古屋・内田橋地区が初の舞台に

国際芸術祭「 あいち 2028」の会期と会場が発表された。2028年9月16日から12月3日まで、愛知芸術文化センターに加え、初の主会場となる半田市と名古屋市南区の内田橋地区を舞台に開催される。

3年ごとに開催される国際芸術祭「 あいち 」の次回展「あいち2028」の会期と会場が、11月10日に発表された。会期は2028年9月16日（土）から12月3日（日）までの79日間。愛知芸術文化センター、半田市、名古屋市南区の内田橋地区を主な会場として開催される。

愛知芸術文化センターは、2010年の初開催以来、毎回会場となってきた。1992年に名古屋市中心部に開館した複合文化施設で、国内外の20世紀美術を中心とする充実したコレクションを擁する愛知県美術館、大ホールやコンサートホール、小ホールなどを備えた愛知県芸術劇場、アートスペースとアートプラザで構成される愛知県文化情報センターからなる。

今回初めて主会場となる半田市は、名古屋市中心部から南へ約25キロに位置する、知多半島の中心都市だ。天然の良港である衣浦港を生かし、江戸時代から海運や醸造業で栄え、地域の政治・経済・文化の中核として発展してきた。黒板塀の醸造蔵が並ぶ半田運河や、明治期の産業遺産である半田赤レンガ建物などで知られ、童話「ごんぎつね」の作者・新美南吉が生まれ育った地でもある。

同じく初めて主会場となる内田橋地区は、名古屋市南区の北西部に位置する。かつて周辺には遠浅の海が広がり、江戸時代から交通・水運の要所として栄えた。堀川と新堀川が合流する付近に架かる内田橋のたもとには、昔ながらの風情を残す内田橋商店街が広がる。近年は地域住民や商店主による活性化の取り組みが進み、老舗と新たな店舗が共存するまちとなっている。

会場の決定にあたり、芸術監督のシャビール・フセイン・ムスタファは、プレスリリースで次のようにコメントしている。

「これらの場所を訪れ、それぞれの場所がその歴史をいかにして現在へと繋いできたかに感銘を受けました。愛知芸術文化センターは、文化芸術の交流の場として長らく機能しています。内田橋地区では、地域に親しまれてきた建物やスペースに新たな活用の方法を見出す人々と出会いました。半田市では、長く続く醸造と発酵の文化が、まちなかの建物や運河にその歴史を刻んでいます。

アーティストや『あいち2028』のチームをはじめとした仲間たち、そして地域のコミュニティと協働すること、また、これらの出会いを通じてなにが形作られていくかを楽しみにしています」

article_text:
Tilda Swinton and Emma Mackey , “ Narnia ‘s” White Witches of past and present, were both on hand at the Marrakech Film Festival opening ceremony on Friday night.

Swinton played the character in the original “Chronicles of Narnia” film trilogy, whereas Mackey — who is serving on the festival’s jury — takes on the role in Greta Gerwig’s upcoming “The Magician’s Nephew” movie at Netflix.

Related Stories

Liam Neeson Says There's 'Nobody Better Than' Meryl Streep to Take Over Aslan Role in ‘Narnia,' but Admits He Didn't Know About Greta Gerwig's Movie: 'This Is News to Me'

'Narnia' White Witches Tilda Swinton and Emma Mackey Excited to Meet for the First Time at Marrakech Film Festival: 'My Absolute Dream'

Speaking to Variety on the red carpet, Swinton — who served as Marrakech jury president in 2019 — said she hasn’t yet met Mackey, but hopes to say hello this weekend. “I don’t know her … I’ll say, ‘I don’t know you, but nice to meet you!'” she said. “I’m excited for her.”

Mackey, on the other hand, said they have a group dinner planned for Saturday night, where they’ll officially meet for the first time. “It’s thrilling, my absolute dream person,” she said.

Does Mackey plan to ask Swinton for any advice? “I mean, what would I… She’s the queen. I wouldn’t even know how to breathe around her, I don’t think. So step by step.”

As for her role on the jury, Mackey said: “I’m just so happy to be here.”

“I love that it’s a festival that honors first and second time filmmakers. I think it’s very smart,” she continued. “You know how hard it is to make a movie and get them financed and how miraculous it is to get everything aligned, so I’m very hopeful and I’m happy to be a part of that.”

This year’s edition of Marrakech Film Festival is presided over by Marion Cotillard, with jurors joining Mackey including “Phantom Thread” star Vicky Krieps, Danish actor Claes Bang, French actor-director Gilles Lellouche, “The Voice of Hind Rajab” helmer Kaouther Ben Hania, “All of Us Strangers” filmmaker Andrew Haigh, Franco-Senegalese helmer Ramata-Toulaye Sy and Moroccan director-producer Saïd Hamich Benlarbi.

Asked by Variety her mindset going into leading the jury, Cotillard said she thinks they will be a “simple audience.”

“I don’t want to have a mission or to expect anything — I expect good movies and to be moved and to be questioned, obviously, but just to enjoy watching movies together and talk about it,” she said.

The Oscar winner was similarly passionate in her speech during the ceremony, in which she posed the question: “Does a competition between artists really make sense?”

“The way we experience a film is so personal that what moves one of us may deeply resonate in a completely different way with someone else,” she added. “But a film festival is also, and above all, a way of shining a light. And these films, especially first and second films, need that light, that attention and that recognition. Making a film is an act of courage.”

Cotillard, whose work has spanned French arthouse films and Hollywood fare like “The Dark Night Rises” and “Inception,” has recently been the subject of fancasting for the new James Bond film starring Robert Pattinson. But when asked about the prospect on the red carpet, she kept mum: “Oh my God, I have no answer!”

The festival opened with Jesse Eisenberg’s musical comedy “The Debut,” starring Julianne Moore in an Oscar-tipped performance as a shy housewife who is forced out of her shell when she auditions for a regional theater production.

Though neither Eisenberg nor Moore were present on Friday, the director sent through a short video message that was played before the screening. “The film is kind of autobiographical — it’s about my love for community theater, which changed my life,” he said. “I hope you love it too and that you watch it communally, which is the way it was meant to be seen. Thank you so much.”

Festival director Mélita Toscan du Plantier said “it’s a shame” that Eisenberg and Moore couldn’t be at the fest, but acknowledged that “they are touring for the Oscars.”

“It’s a movie that everybody talks about, but we are proud to show the movie and I think people are going to like it,” she said.

Toscan du Plantier also pointed out that “Artificial” will screen as part of the festival next week, with director Luca Guadagnino on hand and participating in a masterclass. “It has been seen only one screening in New York and only one screening in London, so it’s a big gift for the people of Morocco to see it,” she added. “I had to sign an NDA when I saw it!”

The Marrakech Film Festival runs through Nov. 28.

article_text:
Months after a “ How the Grinch Stole Christmas ” sequel was announced, director Ron Howard is setting the record straight on what it would take for the follow-up film to actually come to fruition.

“I just have to caution everybody that Jim [Carrey] and I aren’t gonna go forward unless we think we have a great script, and we don’t even have a script right now,” Howard told People . “We have really good writers and an idea that I’m excited about that I think is very much in keeping with the spirit of Dr. Seuss, his blend of comedy and fantasy. So I’m very pleased with what we have to work with, but I don’t wanna make any promises that it’s happening because Jim and I are aligned on one thing — we’re not gonna go forward unless we believe it has a chance to be great.”

Related Stories

Russell Brand Takes the Stand in Rape Trial and Reveals No One Agreed to Testify on His Behalf: 'My Entire Life Has Been Consumed by These Allegations'

Russell Brand Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison After Rape, Sexual Assault Convictions

Howard continued, noting that the duo feels so “proud of the original movie.” “We feel so fortunate, because it takes a little bit of luck for a movie to come together and become an evergreen the way that film has. And the following, the fact that it’s become a tradition in a lot of households is something that means a great deal to all of us involved, Jim and I in particular.”

But Howard isn’t ruling out a sequel in its eternity. “We’re gonna move cautiously but hopefully toward another movie because we both believe in the premise,” he said. “With a little luck, we’ll get to revisit that world.”

The original Christmas classic first premiered back in 2000 and was a box office hit, earning more than $350 million. Carrey, who starred as the Grinch and would reprise his role for the sequel, has long been outspoken about the toll the specific effects makeup needed to transform into the green creature took on him.

Last year, Howard told Vulture that the actor “started having panic attacks” during the early days of filming because of how uncomfortable the transformation was on his body, adding: “I would see him lying down on the floor in between setups with a brown paper bag. Literally on the floor. He was miserable.” Howard also revealed that Carrey was “ready to give his” $20 million salary back.

article_text:
In 1963, the photographer Dmitri Kasterine heard that Stanley Kubrick was in London filming Dr Strangelove. Kasterine was a fan, so he approached the editor of Queen magazine and successfully pitched a feature on the director at work. Kubrick noticed him on set and said: “Would you like to come and work for me? You stand in the right place.”

Kasterine worked for Kubrick from 1963 to 1971, taking the stills on Dr Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey and A Clockwork Orange. Kubrick taught the photographer the importance of courage, patience and perseverance.

These lessons supplemented his photographic craft, honed since the beginning of the 1960s, creating a style that led to Kasterine, who has died aged 94, becoming one of the most significant portrait photographers of the 70s and 80s. He photographed James Baldwin, Michael Caine, Patricia Highsmith , Martin and Kingsley Amis , Tom Stoppard and Queen Elizabeth II for Harpers & Queen, Vogue, the BBC’s Radio Times and the Daily Telegraph magazine.

In his work, Kasterine wanted to “avoid the conventional” and prevent the sitter from “putting on a polite face”. He utilised his gentlemanly charm and elegance, putting the subject at ease before turning away, pretending to adjust his equipment, ignoring the sitter – attempting to catch them off guard, thus revealing something of themselves. This approach unveiled vulnerability in Dirk Bogarde , discomfort in Samuel Beckett and boredom in Muriel Spark .

In an interview with the reporter Bradley Towle, Kasterine said: “I look for something that gives me a shock. I look for something that has unusual elements. It could be what they’re wearing; it could be the background. It could be just an expression. I don’t really look for it, it comes to me.”

As well as his acclaimed portraits of the literati, he took great pride in a personal project undertaken between 1996 and 2018 in his adopted home of New York state. He had become fascinated with the city of Newburgh on the Hudson River, which, from being awarded the title of All American City by Look magazine in 1952, had become, by the 1990s, blighted by recession, corruption and racism. He set about to capture the decaying splendour of the city and, more importantly, the dignity of the overlooked, predominantly Black community that called it home.

In the introduction to his 2012 book, Newburgh: Portrait of a City, Kasterine wrote: “This is a record of uncelebrated and ignored people … But in the ruins of the buildings and in the faces of the people I see warmth and beauty, and in some of the faces a determination to change things.” Three years later, Kasterine filmed a documentary, Newburgh: Beauty and Tragedy . The city embraced his work, and 44 of his Newburgh portraits were mounted on the exterior of its Ritz theatre, from 2012 to 2026.

His photographs are held by the Royal Collection Trust and the National Portrait Gallery in London, and the Smithsonian Institution’s National Portrait Gallery in Washington DC.

Dmitri’s father, Nicolas Kasterine, had served in the Russian Imperial Guard and was the aide-de-camp to the Grand Duke Dmitri Pavlovich, who was involved in the assassination of Grigori Rasputin. Having fought the Bolsheviks in the 1917 revolution, Nicolas escaped Russia via Finland, bringing with him a large, uncut diamond, which, when in London, he sold to buy a suit and a sports car. There, Nicolas married Katherine White, the daughter of an insurance broker, and the young couple socialised with other Russian émigrés in Paris, Monte Carlo (where Dmitri’s elder sister, Irina, was born), and London.

The young family then settled in the village of Kemsing, near Sevenoaks, Kent, where Dmitri was born, named after his godfather, the grand duke. Kasterine’s parents divorced in 1935, and Katherine took her two children to live outside the village of Westerham, also in Kent. Nicolas died in a car crash the following year.

The second world war was a frightening experience for the sensitive Dmitri. Being close to Biggin Hill aerodrome, Westerham was frequently bombed by the Luftwaffe, and on his eighth birthday, bombs fell so close that the house was badly damaged.

When the air raids stopped, Katherine put up a bird table outside the kitchen window. Dmitri wanted to photograph the birds, so his mother bought him a camera. He built a dark room and excitedly developed the film. When he saw that the birds were pinpricks in the frame, he burst into tears. Undeterred, he moved on to cows in the fields, with excellent results.

After the war, Dmitri was sent to board at Radley college in Oxfordshire, where he remained until 1950. It was while at school that he learned of his mother’s death in a riding accident in 1948. He was just 15.

After leaving Radley and working briefly as a wine merchant and then for Lloyd’s of London, Kasterine, who had inherited a love of fast cars from his father, took up motor racing. In 1956, he suffered a life-threatening injury when the Lotus-Bristol racing car he was driving at the Aintree International meeting overturned and crashed through the safety barrier. A friend visited while he was recovering in hospital and suggested he take up flying. He did, and for a while he worked as a commercial pilot flying to Australia.

On a stopover in Karachi, Kasterine photographed the breaking-in of a young thoroughbred. Pleased with the result, and frightened of flying, Kasterine decided to take up photography professionally.

In London from 1961, Kasterine shared a studio with the photographer Michael Wallis, who mentored both Kasterine and their dark-room assistant, Patrick Lichfield . Dmitri hustled for work from magazines and sought out public figures to request a sitting, and his career took off.

In 1981 his first book, England and the English, was published. This gentle collection of portraits, daily life and landscapes was a swansong to the bucolic ideal of his native land. He needed a new challenge.

He had been to the US once, to photograph Mick Jagger in Los Angeles in 1975, and had visited New York City on the way home. He liked it, and moved there in 1984. There, he shot celebrated portraits of art-world luminaries such as Jean-Michel Basquiat , Roy Lichtenstein and Cindy Sherman , and commissions for the Sunday New York Times.

In his later years Kasterine moved to Garrison, in the wilds of New York state, with his second wife, Caroline (nee Cristofalo), whom he had married in 1988. There he took pictures of farmers and people who loved horses, and in 2021 he published a collection of his work, Who How When Where. After seven decades taking photographs, he was, he told Towle, still “… always on the lookout … It’s very difficult to explain exactly why and wherefore I take a picture, but it’s a silence; it’s a tap on the shoulder.”

He is survived by Caroline and their son, Nicholas; his children, Alexander and Cathy, from his 1963 marriage to Elizabeth Dickson, which ended in divorce, a daughter, Lucie, from a relationship with Frances Pemberton, and six grandchildren.

title_original: An Eva Gonzalès Retrospective Puts the Non-Impressionist Artist Back on the Map
editorial_title_zh: 一场伊娃·冈萨雷斯回顾展让这位非印象派艺术家重回大众视野
editorial_excerpt_zh: “这场展览绝不把她呈现为印象派画家，”展览联合策展人斯蒂法妮·坎塔鲁蒂（Stéphanie Cantarutti）告诉ARTnews。

Impressionniste）节的一部分组织一场展览，但因疫情而搁置，直到小皇宫（Petit Palais）接手，并在那里举办了“伊娃·冈萨雷斯（1847–1883）：一个自由精神艺术家的旅程”（“Eva Gonzalès (1847–1883): A Free-Spirited Artist’s Journey”），展出将持续到1月。", "links": [{"text": "Eva ）。身为家庭好友的小说家兼记者阿尔芒·拉潘特（Armand Lapointe）称这幅肖像画是个失败，并指责冈萨雷斯同意给马奈做模特。具有讽刺意味的是，在1874年她首次以马奈学生的身份在沙龙登记的那一年，她提交的描绘剧院包厢中坐着一男一女的作品《意大利剧院包厢》却遭到评审团的拒绝。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为什么在关于19世纪末法国艺术的大多数历史叙述中几乎见不到冈萨雷斯的身影？展览表明她在生前享有相当高的声誉，让-雷蒙德·盖拉尔也尽其所能让世人记住他母亲的贡献。但据坎塔鲁蒂所言，与于连·马奈（柏特·莫里索的女儿）不同，只有他一人在努力维系冈萨雷斯的遗产。于连·马奈身边环绕着斯特凡·马拉美、克劳德·莫奈和埃德加·德加等人物，他们帮助她提升了莫里索作为杰出印象派画家的地位；她的丈夫欧仁·鲁阿尔（Ernest rose），这是一幅创作于1874年、于1885年被法国国家收购的粉彩画。直到135年后的2021年，小皇宫才购得油画《女仆》或《在栅栏旁》（La Servante ou À la barrière，约1865-70年）。（坎塔鲁蒂指出：“她的绝大多数作品现在都收藏在私人手中，散落于法国国内外。”）", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "冈萨雷斯经常被置于与其他人的关系中来描述——作为某人的女儿或某人的学生——人们对她与这个艺术和文学圈子的联系大加渲染。“然而，令我印象深刻的是，她本身就非常有吸引力，”坎塔鲁蒂说道，她将此次展览视为迈向更多认可和研究的第一步，“拥有包括大约三分之二她本人作品在内的上百件展品，我们从未如此贴近地还原1885年回顾展的规模。这是公众发现她是一位多么杰出的艺术家的好机会——我想大家会感到惊喜的。”", article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "A retrospective for Eva Gonzalès , who is today best known as Édouard Manet’s only formal pupil, has been long overdue. That correction was planned for 2020, when the Château-Musée de Dieppe was to organize a show as part of the Normandie Impressionniste festival, but it was put on hold by the pandemic until the Petit Palais took up the mantle, where “Eva Gonzalès (1847–1883): A Free-Spirited Artist’s Journey” is on view until January.", "links": [{"text": "Eva Gonzalès", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/eva-gonzales/"}, {"text": "Petit Palais", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/petit-palais/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The six-year delay turned out to be fortuitous, according to cocurator Stéphanie Cantarutti. Now, Manet’s Portrait of Eva Gonzalès (1870) from the National Gallery and Gonzalès’s Une loge aux Italiens (ca. 1874) from the Musée d’Orsay, can be included, as can Gonzalès’s Le Moineau (ca. 1865-70), which the curatorial team managed to track down after decades of its whereabouts being unknown. article_text:
A retrospective for Eva Gonzalès , who is today best known as Édouard Manet’s only formal pupil, has been long overdue. That correction was planned for 2020, when the Château-Musée de Dieppe was to organize a show as part of the Normandie Impressionniste festival, but it was put on hold by the pandemic until the Petit Palais took up the mantle, where “Eva Gonzalès (1847–1883): A Free-Spirited Artist’s Journey” is on view until January.

The six-year delay turned out to be fortuitous, according to cocurator Stéphanie Cantarutti. Now, Manet’s Portrait of Eva Gonzalès (1870) from the National Gallery and Gonzalès’s Une loge aux Italiens (ca. 1874) from the Musée d’Orsay, can be included, as can Gonzalès’s Le Moineau (ca. 1865-70), which the curatorial team managed to track down after decades of its whereabouts being unknown. One of some 70 works by her now on view, that delicate portrait of a young girl with a sparrow shows her mastery in pastel. “In the end, time worked in our favor,” Cantarutti told ARTnews .

The exhibition brings further discoveries, including a revision of the artist’s birth year. “What tipped us off was the way the date was written on the birth certificate,” Cantarutti said. “After taking a closer look at the document, we realized that she had been born in 1847, not 1849.” In-depth research also led to the redating and renaming of several paintings: La Fenêtre (1869–70), for example, was renamed Le Catéchisme , while La Psyché , now dated to 1868–69, had previously been dated to 1869–70.

For more than a century, since critic Camille Laurent Mauclair associated Gonzalès with Impressionism in 1904, the artist’s work has regularly been assessed and reassessed through this lens. A 1993 exhibition at Paris’s Musée Marmottan Monet, which presented her alongside Impressionism’s two most famous women artists, Mary Cassatt and Berthe Morisot, was instrumental in reinforcing this association. The Petit Palais exhibition, however, takes a different approach.

“I am personally opposed to this affiliation,” Cantarutti said. “I fought to ensure that the term ‘Impressionism’ would not appear in any communication materials. The exhibition in no way presents her as an Impressionist.”

There is art historical truth to that statement, as Gonzalès never participated in any of the Impressionist exhibitions. “Her strategy was, like Manet’s, to establish herself at the Salon,” conservator Marianne Mathieu said, noting that Berthe Morisot, against Manet’s advice, turned her back on the Salon and joined the cooperative society whose members would soon become known as the Impressionists.

Gonzalès and Morisot had much in common: They came from cultivated bourgeois families, were criticized for their fierce independence, used their sisters as models, continued to sign their maiden names after marriage, and were close friends with Manet. Morisot, however, further resisted Manet’s tutelage all the more after he substantially retouched one of her paintings in 1870, whereas Gonzalès would ultimately embrace his guidance. “Morisot sought to emancipate herself from the very idea of artistic affiliation, even if that meant becoming part of an emerging avant-garde,” added Mathieu. “Gonzalès, by contrast, boldly claimed her allegiance to Manet, who was a controversial figure at the time.”

The Gonzalès retrospective also raises the question of why this allegiance remained largely concealed for part of her early career. Gonzalès left the studio of Charles Chaplin, her first teacher who did not think a single woman should have her own studio, in 1868 and became Manet’s pupil the following year, after the two met at the salon of painter Alfred Stevens. Gonzalès’s pedagogical roots were further muddied when she submitted to the 1870 Salon. She registered as Chaplin’s pupil, but Enfant de troupe (1869–70) , one of two paintings selected, clearly drew on Manet’s Le Fifre (1866) . Depicting a young boy in military uniform holding a bugle against a dark, neutral background, Enfant de troupe was acquired by the French State, the only work of hers to enter a public collection during her lifetime, and the acquisition likely owed much to the connections of her father, prominent writer Emmanuel Gonzalès.

Further complicating the situation, Manet exhibited at the 1870 Salon his 6.25-foot-tall Portrait d’Eva Gonzalès . The novelist and journalist Armand Lapointe, a family friend, called the portrait a failure and reproached Gonzalès for having agreed to sit for Manet. Ironically, in 1874, the first year she came registered as Manet’s pupil at the Salon, her submission, Une loge aux Italiens , of a man and woman seated in a theater box, was rejected by the jury.

It is difficult to assess Gonzalès’s style, as she died too young—at 36, with the revised birth year—to reveal the full extent of her abilities. She confined herself to the subjects traditionally deemed appropriate for women artists at the time: portraits of family and friends, scenes of domestic life and leisure, and still lifes. Such subjects helped her avoid controversy and establish a reputation. According to critic Jean-Marie Tasset, “Behind her intimate scenes and landscapes lies a fierce energy, a blazing fire that reveals itself as soon as Eva sets her brush to canvas. All the dark magic of the blue note.” Under Manet’s aegis, her style grew more spontaneous. How brightly and freely her flame might have burned had she lived longer remains an open question.

At the Petit Palais, visitors follow a broadly chronological path through Gonzalès’s career, with thematic digressions exploring her relationship with her husband, Henri Guérard, and their artistic partnership, including time spent together in Normandy. A renowned beauty with a slender figure and an elegant wardrobe evocative of her social status, Gonzalès had rejected eligible suitors before falling in love with Guérard, a talented engraver who collaborated with Manet, Paul Gachet, Camille Pissarro, and Paul Cezanne, among others. The couple married in 1879 and remained together until Gonzalès’s death in 1883. Guérard later remarried his sister-in-law Jeanne, which Gonzalès seems to have predicted in her rejected-Salon painting, Une loge aux Italiens : the man and woman are, in fact, Guérard and Jeanne. “There is material for a great movie scenario, for sure,” Cantarutti said. “We, however, chose to stick to the facts.”

The final section unfolds in two parts. One looks beyond Gonzalès’s death, bringing together pastels of Jeanne posing in Eva’s wedding dress (perhaps another premonition on Gonzalès’s part), photographs of Gonzalès’s 1885 posthumous retrospective, and a Norbert Goeneutte portrait of Eva’s son, Jean-Raimond.

The other half focuses on the artist’s final works, including Miss et Bébé (1877–78) featuring a nanny watching over a little girl. “We can see the evolution from the porcelain-like finish of compositions in the style of Chaplin toward a more energetic touch,” Cantarutti said. “In unfixed pastel-on-canvas works held in the United States, her use of increasingly bold colors is striking, along with a greater freedom in her brushwork.” In Pommes d’Api , which is owned by the Minneapolis Institute of Art and was too fragile to bring to Paris, the brightness of Gonzalès’s reds and yellows convey the apples’ acidity.

What accounts Gonzalès’s near absence from most art historical tellings of late 19th-century French art? The exhibition shows that she enjoyed considerable success during her lifetime, and Jean-Raimond Guérard tried to keep the contributions of his mother in the conversation as much as he could. But unlike Julie Manet, Berthe Morisot’s daughter, he alone was working to keep alive Gonzalès’s legacy, according to Cantarutti. Julie Manet was surrounded by figures like Stéphane Mallarmé, Claude Monet, and Edgar Degas, who helped her elevate Morisot’s status as a preeminent Impressionist, as did her husband, Ernest Rouart, who was at the same time fighting to secure recognition for his father’s collection and work.

Cantarutti offered a second reason: “She is not that heavily represented in French national museums.” The Musée d’Orsay has La Matinée rose ( The Pink Morning ), a 1874 pastel acquired by the French state in 1885. More than 135 years would pass before the Petit Palais purchased the oil painting La Servante or À la barrière (ca. 1865-70) in 2021. (“Most of her works are now in private collections, scattered across France and abroad,” Cantarutti noted.)

Gonzalès has often been described in relation to others—as someone’s daughter or someone’s pupil—and much has been made of the connections that linked her to this artistic and literary milieu. “What struck me, however, was that she was interesting in her own right,” said Cantarutti, who sees the exhibition as a first step toward more recognition and research. “With more than a hundred works, including roughly two-thirds by her, we have never been so close to recreating the scale of the 1885 retrospective. It is a chance for the public to discover what a remarkable artist she was—and I think people will be pleasantly surprised.”

“我们可以看到从肖像像像的完成作品在查普林的风格的进化,到一个更能量的触摸,”Cantarutti说,“在美国举行的无缝的 pastel-on-canvas工作中,她的使用越来越勇敢的颜色是令人震惊的,以及在她的刷子中更大的自由。由明尼亚波利斯艺术研究所,并且太脆弱地带到巴黎,甘萨莱斯的红色和黄色的亮度传递了苹果的酸性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20_Eva_Gonzales_Nounou_avec_enfant_1877-1878.jpg?w=400", "alt": "一个白色衣服的女人在地板上的伞旁边的画,一个小女孩站在一个开放的门口。", "caption": "Eva Gonzales, Miss et bébé, 饰演 饰演 1877 - 78 国立艺术画廊,华盛顿,公元", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "戈纳扎尔在19世纪末的法国艺术史上几乎没有什么?展览表明,她在她一生中取得了相当大的成功,而珍·雷蒙德·盖拉德试图尽可能地保持母亲的贡献。莫内特和埃德加·德加斯,谁帮助她的高级莫里索特的地位作为一个突出印象主义者,就像她的丈夫,埃尔内斯特·鲁亚特,谁同时正在努力确保认可他的父亲的收藏和工作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "坎塔鲁蒂提出了第二个理由:“她不是法国国家博物馆中如此重演。 1874 法國國家購買的蛋糕 1885 更多 比 135 小宫购买油画La Servante或 À la barrière之前的几年会过去。 (ca. 1865-70) 在 2021 “她现在的大多数作品都是私人收藏品,遍布法国和国外,”Cantarutti指出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/19_Eva_Gonzales_La_Promenade_a_ane_1880.png?w=400", "alt": "一幅蓝色衣服的女人的画,坐在一匹马上,握着她的鼻子,站着的男人看着她。", "caption": "Eva Gonzalès, La Promenade à âne (Henri et Jeanne) , 1880–82. 照片 David Emeney/Bristol Museum & Archives", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Gonzalès 经常被描述在与其他人 - 作为某人的女儿或某人的学生 - 并从她与这个艺术和文学环境联系的联系中得到了很多东西,“但我感到震惊的是,她对自己的兴趣,”Cantarutti说,他认为展览是向更多的认可和研究迈出的第一步。 1885这是一个机会,公众发现她是什么令人惊叹的艺术家,我认为人们会很愉快地惊讶。", "translated": true}]

連続テレビ小説「ブラッサム」

＜総合＞【毎週月曜～土曜】 午前8時～8時15分＊土曜は1週間を振り返ります ＜NHK BS＞【毎週月曜～金曜】午前7時30分～7時45分 ＜BSP4K＞【毎週月曜～金曜】午前7時30分～7時45分

【作】 櫻井 剛、小松與志子 【音楽】 fox capture plan 【主題歌】 「咲き誇れ」 YOASOBI 【出演】 石橋静河、加賀まりこ、松たか子、国仲涼子、渡部篤郎 ほか 【スタッフ】 制作統括：村山峻平、櫻井壮一 プロデューサー：大野陽平 演出：盆子原 誠、中泉 慧、佐藤玲衣、田中陽児、小林直毅、野田雄介

公式サイト 公式X 公式Instagram

第６週 「ふたり、北へ」

お腹に赤ん坊が宿っていることが分かり、喜ぶ珠（石橋静河）と保（金子大地）。しかし、保が大学に通いながら生活費をどう工面するかなど、考えなければいけない問題は山積みであった。そんな中、札幌の銀行に勤める保の親戚、木村正吾（三宅弘城）が照子（山田真歩）と一緒に突然、訪ねてくる。照子と正吾は、珠と保に必要な出産費用や生活費の援助をすることを条件に、あることを珠たちに提案する。
